14.7: 14.7 With an oath. Perhaps he swore to this end, that he might provide an occasion by which he would seem to do unwillingly what he did willingly. For he would not have fulfilled this for someone he loved, as he fulfilled it for the prophet; and he would have done it earlier, if he could have done so with an excuse. BEDE. If we happen perhaps to have sworn incautiously, etc., down to nor did he grieve that he had incurred any guilt by such a perjury. ISIDORE. An oath by which evil is incautiously promised is not to be kept, as if, etc., down to for it is more tolerable not to fulfil the oath than to remain in debauchery.
14.9: 14.9 Was saddened. As it appeared to those at table. For such was the sadness of Herod as was the repentance of Pharaoh.
14.10: 14.10 And he beheaded. John was diminished by the head, Christ was exalted on the cross: because the fame of the former decreased, that of the latter grew; hence: He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3). In the severed head of John it is shown that the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of all the prophets. Morally. The death of John signifies the end of the law, which having ended, one rightly passes over to Christ, who is the end of the law unto justice for everyone who believes.
14.13: 14.13 When Jesus heard this. After the law and the prophet lost their head and voice among the Jews, Jesus passes to the desert, the place of the Church, which before had no husband. He withdrew. He did not flee from fear, but withdrew, sparing his enemies lest they join murder to murder, giving an example of avoiding rashness. Or he withdrew to test the faith of those who believed; hence: And when the crowds heard, etc. On foot. By their own labor, to show the ardor of their mind. They leave the cities, that is, their former ways of life. They have the will, but not the strength to arrive. Therefore Jesus goes out to meet them, and in pity heals, so that full faith may immediately have its reward. See how much he is delighted by the devotion of believers.
14.15: 14.15 And when evening had come, etc. Jesus leaves Judea, goes into the desert, the crowds follow, and he meets and heals them. This is not in the morning or at midday, but in the evening, when the sun of justice has set and the end of the world has drawn near. His disciples. Carnal men, ignorant of the coming miracle of the feeding, to whom it had been said: Do not go into the way of the Gentiles (Matthew 10). Mystically. The Jews loathe that the Gentiles are received and murmur; Isaiah uses their voice (Isaiah 40): Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket. Again: All the nations are as if they were not, but they are before him. But the Lord decided to feed them through the apostles; hence he adds: But Jesus, etc. Send away the crowds. It is long since they have followed idols, and therefore they are not to be fed by us with the bread of the word of God.
14.16: 14.16 Give them. He challenges them to give, so that, as they testify that they have nothing, the greatness of the sign may be better known; where he also hints that the hungry hearts are to be fed through them.
14.17: 14.17 Five loaves and two fishes. By the five loaves and two fishes the whole Old Testament is signified. By the five loaves, the five books of Moses, which are rightly of barley, which is the food of beasts of burden, for to the unlearned rough and coarse things are to be given. For the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 1). Yet within lies hidden the marrow of the sweetest meaning. By the two fishes, the prophets and the psalms; hence after the resurrection he says: What is written in the law and in the prophets and the many places concerning me (Luke 24).
14.19: 14.19 Taking the five, etc. He took the five loaves; he did not create new ones, because coming in the flesh he preached nothing other than what had been foretold, and fulfilled it in deed. He blessed. When he opened their mind to understand the Scriptures, he multiplied by the gift of inner sweetness. He broke when he brought the mysteries of the law into the midst.
14.20: 14.20 The leftovers. The more hidden things, which cannot be grasped by the unlearned, are not to be neglected, but are to be diligently sought out by the twelve apostles, who are signified by the twelve baskets, and by their successors. Baskets are used for servile work. And God chose the weak things of the world, to confound the strong (1 Corinthians 1).
14.21: 14.21 Besides women and children. The frail sex and the lesser age are unworthy of being counted. It signifies the weak in faith, not yet fit for battle.
14.22: 14.22 And immediately he compelled, etc. RABANUS. Those who, as John says, were about to come to make him king (John 6), who had seen the miracle of the loaves, etc., down to for them let us pray, that they may not soften us.
14.23: 14.23 He went up. He fed the crowd as God, he went up to pray as man. Not that he did not have all things in his power, but to fulfil the form of man. In this is the duty of piety; there follows the remarkable miracle of power. And when evening came. This storm is rightly said to be in the evening, because when the Church is in tribulation she is said to be as if in night, and the sun of justice seems to have hidden itself.
14.24: 14.24 But the boat. The ship in the middle of the sea, Jesus alone on land: because sometimes the Church is so, not only afflicted but even disfigured, that she seems altogether abandoned by God; but God does not abandon her. Hence Mark says: He saw them laboring in rowing (Mark 6). Though not present, and though he delays, yet he sees and strengthens.
14.25: 14.25 But in the fourth. They are in danger the whole night, because when a man considers himself he finds nothing but the darkness of distress and the heat of enemies. He came to them. Mark says: Wishing to pass them by, yet it was for their deliverance that he came. This happens so that, troubled for a time but soon freed, they may be the more amazed and give thanks; the same often happens in the sufferings of the saints.
14.26: 14.26 And seeing, etc. Because it often happens that when some calm suddenly arises after long tribulation, true deliverance is not immediately believed. And therefore, while the former fear remains intense, prayer is directed toward deliverance.
14.27: 14.27 It is I, do not be afraid. He does not add who, because they could recognize him from his familiar voice. Or because he is the one who said: He Who Is has sent me to you (Exodus 3).
14.28: 14.28 Lord, if it is you. If you are that deliverer, command me to come, in imitation of you, by overcoming afflictions.
14.29: 14.29 And descending. Despairing of human help, he tramples afflictions in his mind, that he may be conformed to Jesus. He walked, etc. Behold, a man walks on the waters. Therefore do not doubt that Christ is a true body because he walked on the waters. He made him walk on the sea to show divine power. He makes him sink lest he forget his weakness, lest he think himself equal to God, and lest he become proud.
14.30: 14.30 And when he began, etc. He is left for a little while to temptation, that faith may be increased; for as he believed that by his command he could be held up on the waves, so, while sinking, he believed he could be saved by his power.
14.32: 14.32 The wind ceased. Wherever God is present by grace, soon all wars are stilled.
14.33: 14.33 And they worshiped, etc. Having seen the sign, they confess him the Son of God; why then does Arius contend that he is a creature?
14.34: 14.34 Into the land of Gennesaret. Allegorically. Gennesaret is interpreted as garden of princes. Through the type of the apostles and the ship, therefore, we must understand that the Church, delivered from persecutions, is led by the Lord to the shore, that is, to rest, where the inheritance of paradise and the joy of the first robe will be restored.
14.36: 14.36 The hem of his garment, etc. That is, the least commandment, or the flesh by which we come to the Word of God; whoever touches him by believing is healed of every sickness of impiety.
15.1: 15.1 Then there came. The men of Gennesaret, less learned, believe, but those who seem wise come to the fight. CHRYSOSTOM. Then, he says, namely when he had worked innumerable signs, when, etc., down to to show their great malice.
15.2: 15.2 For they do not wash. Those who are polluted within by spite find fault with nothing within. They keep their baptisms in vain who neglect to wash away the filth of their hearts and bodies.
15.3: 15.3 Why do you also. If you despise the commandments of God because of the traditions of men, why do you accuse the disciples, who set aside the commandments of men in order to keep the decrees of God?
15.4: 15.4 Honor your father. JEROME. Honor in the Scriptures is understood not so much in offering greetings and courtesies as, etc., down to so that children should honor their parents also in providing the necessities of life.
15.5: 15.5 But you say, etc. But your tradition is contrary. You compel children to say this to their parents: what I was going to offer to God I consume on food for you, and it profits you, O father, that you fear to eat what is consecrated. Or: what I offer to God profits you yourself. Whoever shall say. That is, he will be worthy of eternal life. Or shall say, that is, it will profit him to say. It will profit. As if he were to say: No, rather you would be sacrilegious if you received it, because I have vowed it to God. Or it will profit you if I have given it to God.
15.7: 15.7 Well did he prophesy, etc. In the Spirit he foretold the pretense of the Jews, that in deceit they opposed the Gospel.
15.8: 15.8 Honors me with their lips. Teacher, we know that you are truthful (Mark 12). Or, by commending outward cleanness, the inner cleanness, which is the true one, is not in them.
15.11: 15.11 Not what enters. There is nothing outside a man that defiles him within, not even food offered to idols, insofar as it is a creature of God; with one saying all superstition of observances is crushed, when religion is thought to lie in the discernment of foods.
15.12: 15.12 Then approaching. The religion of the Pharisees is great in matters of food; having heard this word they were scandalized, that is, were indignant. Were scandalized. In Greek we can render it a stumbling block, or a fall, or a striking of the foot. Hence: Whoever scandalizes anyone, that is, gives occasion of falling.
15.14: 15.14 Let them alone, etc. Leave them to their own judgment, because they are irrecoverable. Hence Paul: Avoid a heretical man after the first and second correction (Titus 3).
15.15: 15.15 Explain. What was said plainly, the apostles think was said by a parable. He is a faulty hearer who wishes to understand obscure things as plain, or plain things as obscure.
15.19: 15.19 From the heart, etc. For they are not sent in by the devil, but are born from one's own will. For the devil is an inciter, not an author, because he does not know interior things except through bearing and gestures.
15.20: 15.20 With unwashed. The sayings of the prophets are spiritual, concerning the chastening of heart and body, such as this: Wash yourselves, be clean (Isaiah 1). The Pharisees understood it carnally, of the body alone, which is vain to do.
15.21: 15.21 And going out, etc. Leaving the slanderers, into the territory of Tyre and Sidon, to free the daughter, and through the faith of a Gentile woman to rebuke the unbelief of the Scribes. The leaving of the slanderers signifies that after the resurrection he would leave the unbelief of the Jews, going through preaching to the Gentiles.
15.22: 15.22 She cried out, etc. She cries out through faith; hence she knew to call him Son of David, confessing the incarnation of Christ. She asks on behalf of her daughter, that is, for her own people not yet believing, that they may be freed from the very deceit of the devil. Or the daughter is the soul or conscience of anyone within the Church enslaved to the devil, for whom mother Church asks, or the man himself for his defiled conscience.
15.23: 15.23 Who did not answer. Not out of pride, but lest he be contrary to his own statement: Do not go into the way of the Gentiles (Matthew 10). Thus he avoids the slander of the Jews, while the salvation of the Gentiles is reserved for the time of the passion and resurrection.
15.24: 15.24 I was not sent. As if he said: First I must fulfil the mystery of my coming among the Jews, and so bring in other sheep; and he does this by deferring the petition of this woman as a sign.
15.26: 15.26 The bread of the children. The word of salvation, which is owed first to the Jews, is not good to give to dogs, or Gentiles, who always bark with canine rage.
15.27: 15.27 Yes, Lord. Under the person of the woman, the wondrous faith, patience, and humility of the Church is proclaimed. Faith, because she believes her daughter can be healed. Patience, because, so often rejected, she persists in her prayers. Humility, because she compares herself not to dogs but to little dogs. For even the little dogs. The table is sacred Scripture; the crumbs of the children are the inner mysteries by which the humble are refreshed under the table: because the Gentiles, humbly subject to the Scriptures, are the little dogs. The little ones eat not the loaves, not the crusts, that is, not the surface of the letter, but the marrow.
15.28: 15.28 Great is your faith. So above of the centurion: I have not found such great faith in Israel (Matthew 8), who likewise (like this Canaanite woman) prefigured the faith of the Gentiles. Great is the faith of the Gentiles, who obey at the hearing of the ear, and obtain salvation in God for themselves and their own. That he heals the centurion's servant and the Canaanite's daughter without coming to them signifies that the Gentiles, to whom he did not come by his presence, are to be saved by his word. And she was healed. Here an example is given of catechizing and baptizing infants, who can neither understand nor do anything, but are freed from the devil by the faith and confession of their parents.
15.29: 15.29 And when he had crossed over. When in the daughter of the Canaanite woman he had prefigured the salvation of the Gentiles, he returns to Judea, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved. Onto a mountain. The Lord on the mountain, the Word sits on high: because in his majesty he could not be understood.
15.30: 15.30 The blind. The blind are those who do not understand, even if they obey those who command. The deaf are those who do not obey, even if they understand.
15.32: 15.32 But Jesus. He calls together the disciples, to teach masters to share their counsels with their juniors. Or that from his speech they may understand the greatness of the sign. I have compassion on the crowd. The crowd waits on the Lord three days, because the faithful who repent turn to the Lord in deed, word, and thought; they would faint on the way of the present life if they were left in their conscience without the food of teaching. In the earlier sign, the nearby places and neighbors, and the five senses, are mentioned, and the Lord does not recall them but the disciples do, in the evening with the sun already declining. Here the Lord says he has compassion, and why: because they have now continued with me three days. In the whole age there is a third time in which grace is given: the first before the law, the second under the law, the third under grace; the fourth is in the future, where there will be day without night, toward which one presses on and is refreshed on the way.
15.33: 15.33 In the desert, loaves. The preachers call the loaves, and themselves the desert, that is, unfruitful. As if they said: Where do we get so much eloquence that we can suffice for such eager hearers?
15.36: 15.36 And taking. To show that he rejoices with men over their salvation, and to instruct us to give thanks even for temporal things. Seven loaves. He feeds by the sevenfold Spirit, with apostolic authority joined, as with the flavor of a few fishes who refresh us by the example of their life or death. The seven loaves are the Scripture of the New Testament, in which the grace of the Holy Spirit is both revealed and given. Nor are they of barley, as above, because here, unlike in the law, the life-giving food of the soul is not covered by figures as by the most tenacious chaff. Here there are not two fishes (as in the law two were anointed, king and priest), but a few, that is, the saints of the New Testament, who have been rescued from the waves of the world, and endure the turbulent sea, and by their example refresh us, lest we faint on the way. BEDE. There it was on the grass, that the desires of the flesh may be suppressed; here on the ground where the world itself, etc., down to both feedings were celebrated on a mountain, because the Scripture of each Testament commands the loftiness of heavenly precepts and rewards: both proclaim the height of Christ. And what was left over. The higher mysteries which the common crowd does not grasp, the apostles lift up and fill seven baskets, that is, the hearts of the perfect, illumined for understanding by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Seven baskets. Baskets are usually woven of rush and palm leaves, and they signify the saints, who place the root of the heart in the very fountain of life, that they may not wither like a rush in water, and who keep in the heart the palm of eternal reward.
15.39: 15.39 And having dismissed the crowd. Here he teaches that preachers, after ministering the word to the crowd, ought themselves to be refreshed within the chamber of the heart with the fruits of virtues. Into the territory. Magedan, which by another name is called Dalmanutha, a region around Gerasa. It is interpreted fruits or messengers, and signifies the garden of which it is said: A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, where the fruits of virtues grow. And there the name of the Lord is proclaimed.
16.1: 16.1 And they came, etc. That he would show a sign from heaven, etc. That he who had fed many with few might rain manna to feed all. Hence John, after the eating of the loaves: What sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? Our fathers ate manna in the desert (John 6). They asked, tempting him, that in the manner of Elijah he would send fire from on high, or like Samuel in summer time make thunder roar, as if they could not slander those too, and say that they happened from the hidden and varied conditions of the air.
1.1: 1.1 Prologue. Matthew, when he had first preached the Gospel in Judea and wished to pass over to the Gentiles, was the first to write the Gospel, in Hebrew, which he left in memory to the brethren from whom he was departing. For as it was necessary to preach the Gospel for the confirmation of the faith, so also to write it against heretics. Although many have written a Gospel, only four have the testimony of authority, because through the four parts of the world they announce the faith of the Trinity, and they are, as it were, the four wheels of the Lord's four-horse chariot, which carries him by the preaching of the Gospel; and the human race, destroyed by a fourfold death, was to be given life by their preaching. Hence the gospels of others fell away and were not received, because they did not want the predetermined number to cease, on account of the power of the mystery. The four evangelists are also designated by four figures, which are not deceptive but conscious to themselves of a joyful mystery. Matthew is understood in the man, because he dwells chiefly on the humanity of Christ. Mark in the lion, because he treats of the resurrection. Luke in the calf, treating of the priesthood. John in the eagle, writing the mysteries of the Divinity. And the Christ whom they describe was a man born of a virgin, a calf in the immolation, a lion in the resurrection, an eagle in the ascension. Or in the man humanity, in the calf the priesthood, in the lion the kingdom, in the eagle the mystery of the Divinity is expressed. The book of the generation. JEROME. The Hebrews give their volumes a name from the beginnings, as the book of Genesis, etc., up to: but this custom is found in many, chiefly in the prophets, as the vision of Isaiah, you understand, this is. Son of David. An inverted order, lest the weaving of the generation be interrupted by Abraham being put first. Of these two he is specially called Son: because one is first among the patriarchs, the other among the kings, to whom the promise concerning Christ was made, so as to show the Jews that Christ would come from the law, in whom they would see the prophecies fulfilled. Son of David, son of Abraham. He chose these two out of all, of whom Christ is called Son, so that to the Jews, to whom he writes, who knew from the law that Christ was to come, it might appear that this is he who had long been promised, in whom all the prophecies were seen to be fulfilled; for to these alone in the Old Testament the promise is read to have been made: And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (Genesis 22). Abraham and David are two pillars standing in the law as in the porch before the door which is Christ; a cord of twelve cubits, that is, the faith of the apostles, encircles them. He embraces in the genealogy these fathers, from the midst of whom the door Christ is opened to believers.
1.2: 1.2 Abraham begot Isaac: and Isaac begot Jacob. The beginning of the generation is fittingly from him to whom it was first promised, in whom is the blessing of all. Matthew begins the generation from the beginning of the promise. And this is carried on even to the end of the book, so that he who was born of this generation may be understood to be God and man. He begins from the beginning, from him to whom the promise of faith was first made, so that in this father they may learn, to whom the promise was first made, who and what kind those ought to be who wish to be blessed in his seed. Matthew begins or computes the generation by descending, because he shows the humanity of Christ, through which God descended to men. Luke, relating by ascending, discloses the form of the sacrament. For beginning from baptism he ascends to God, showing that the baptized ascend to this, that they may be sons of God. Begot. Matthew puts begot: he counts only sons by nature. Luke: Who was: he inserts some sons according to the law or by adoption. Matthew puts begot, and not generated, perhaps that he might be recognized as shown in the end, of whom it is said: This day I have begotten you (Psalm 2). Judah and his brethren. Judah alone is named expressly, so that you may know him from whose stock the promised one was to come. He mentions the brethren of Judah, passing over the brothers of Isaac and Jacob, because those, as aliens, were repelled by the people of God; these, as heirs written in the book of life, and as the twelve patriarchs, in whom the number of the apostles is also signified. But they are not expressed by name, lest the generation extend beyond the number of the mystery. In the seed of the aforesaid fathers Christ entered Egypt; the enemy, foreseeing this, oppressed the people and killed not the women but the males, to extinguish him. From Judah, Christ, whom all nations received; at whose coming Herod, a foreigner, was already ruling.
1.3: 1.3 And Judah. Judah begot Perez and Zerah before he entered Egypt, into which both afterwards passed with their father. And Perez begot Hezron. In Egypt Perez begot Hezron, and Hezron Aram, and Aram Amminadab, and Amminadab Nahshon; and then Moses led them out of Egypt. Nahshon was a leader under Moses in the tribe of Judah through the desert, in which he begot Salmon. This Salmon was a prince in the tribe of Judah, who entered the promised land with Joshua. This Salmon in the promised land begot Boaz by Rahab. Christ is Perez, that is, division, because he will separate the sheep from the goats. He is Hezron, that is, arrow or court, because he pierces the hearts of the hearers. He has also the breadth of charity, by which he loved even his enemies.
1.4: 1.4 And Aram. Aram is interpreted Christ chosen or exalted: Chosen, of whom the prophet says: Behold my servant whom I have chosen (Hosea 11). And elsewhere: The Lord is high above all nations (Psalm 112). He is Amminadab, that is, willing, who says: I will willingly sacrifice to you (Psalm 33). The same is Nahshon, that is, augury, who knows things past, present and future. Or Nahshon, serpentine, because Christ in the manner of a serpent avoided all snares.
1.5: 1.5 And Salmon begot Boaz. Christ is Salmon, that is, sensible, because he perceives all things. He took Rahab, that is, the Church from the Gentiles. Rahab, hunger, or beatitude, or impulse: because the Church of the Gentiles hungers and thirsts for righteousness, and, spread through the whole world, converted philosophers and kings by the impulse of her teaching. Rahab showed the scarlet cord in the window, that is, in the mouth, through confession declares the passion of Christ. Rahab the harlot, who received the messengers of Joshua, whom Salmon, prince of the tribe of Judah, joined to himself, signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which is joined to the prince from Judah, that is, Christ. And she alone with her own is saved, while Jericho, that is, the present age, fortified with seven walls of vices, is encircled for seven days' time by the trumpets of preaching, until at the last trumpet all the walls fall and the last death is destroyed. And Boaz. Boaz is Christ, of whom it is said: Behold the Lord God shall come in strength (Isaiah 40). Note that no holy women are taken into the genealogy of Christ, but those whom Scripture reproves. For he had to be born of sinners, who had come for sinners, that his own might learn that the sins of the fathers do not hurt them. Hence the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be taken from the goats and the sheep, that is, to be generated from the just and from sinners. Of Ruth. The Moabitess, to show that the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth (Isaiah 16). Through her the seed of Abraham is led down to Christ. The Church of the Gentiles, signified by Ruth, before she came to Boaz, that is, to Christ, was of the father the devil. Ruth signifies the Church, which is of Moab, that is, of the Gentiles, who are of the father the devil and of the rock of the desert because of idolatry, from which God raised up children to Abraham; forgetful of her former nation, she comes to Boaz, who is called strong, that is, to Christ, who raises up the seed of his brother, that is, of Moses, who died without children, because the law brought nothing to perfection (Hebrews 7). Ruth, seeing or hastening; because the Church with a pure heart sees God, and hastens to the prize of the heavenly vision, and resolves to persevere in faith and love. And Jesse. The father of David is more often named Isai, but he had two names. Here he is called Jesse, so that one may know that he had come, of whom Isaiah says: A rod shall come forth out of the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11), etc. This is the flower which Isaac smells, saying: Behold the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field (Genesis 27), because the Spirit filled him most abundantly. King. Not that he alone is king in this genealogy, but because he is the first king from Judah and the beginning of kings, on account of whom the others also are kept on the throne of the kingdom; and through this one the order of the generation runs down to Christ, who has the kingdom of David.
1.6: 1.6 And King David. Mystically, David is Christ, who overcame Goliath, that is, the devil. He is strong of hand, or desirable to behold. Of him it is said: The Lord strong and mighty (Psalm 23), etc. And again: Beautiful in form above the sons of men (Psalm 44). Of Uriah. Uriah, that is, my light, God, that is, the devil, who said: I will be like the Most High (Isaiah 14); the Church was joined to him in marriage, and Christ fell in love with her from the high chamber of the Father's majesty, and made her beautiful and joined her to himself in marriage. Uriah, who is a figure of the devil, is interpreted my light, God, who even now transforms himself into an angel of light and makes himself the light of God.
1.7: 1.7 And Solomon. Christ is Solomon, that is, peaceful, because he is our peace, who made both one. He is Rehoboam, that is, the impulse of the people, who swiftly converts peoples to the faith. Rehoboam. Of him it is said: I will give him Rehoboam, the tribe of Judah, that a lamp may remain for David all days in Israel (3 Kings 11). This cannot be taken literally, since Israel did not endure all days, nor was there any leader of David's line in Israel after Christ. But Christ is the eternal lamp in the heavenly Israel, and therefore he is preserved forever. Christ is said to sit upon the throne of David, because David's temporal kingdom prefigured the eternal kingdom of Christ. Abijah. Father the Lord, that is, Christ, who says: I will be a Father to him, because as Lord he did whatsoever he willed (Psalm 113). He is also Asa, that is, lifting up, because he took away the sins of the world.
1.8: 1.8 Jehoshaphat, etc. Judging, or the judgment of God, namely Christ, who judges the world of the earth in equity. And he begot Joram. Christ is Joram, that is, exalted, who says: No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven (John 3).
1.9: 1.9 And Uzziah. Under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, Isaiah prophesied about Christ. Because of the sins of the rulers the mouths of the prophets were shut. Hezekiah. The strong Lord; he is the one who says to the apostles: Do not be afraid. To Hezekiah, when he was without children, it was said: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live (Isaiah 38). So he wept, not because of a longer life, since he knew that Solomon had pleased God in this by not asking for more years, but because he doubted whether the promise of God would be fulfilled, since he knew he was of the line of David, through whom Christ had to come, and he himself was without children; hence he also said: I shall not see the Lord God, and again, I shall behold man no more, etc. On the other hand, he believed, because he who promised is faithful. But God changes the sentence he had given, to test faith, and grants a span for begetting.
1.10: 1.10 Manasseh. Forgetful. He is the one who said, as if to the converted sinner: I will not remember all his iniquities (Ezekiel 18). Amon, that is, faithful or nourisher, signifying Christ, of whom it is said: The Lord is faithful in all his ways, who gathers his children as a hen her chicks (Psalm 144).
1.11: 1.11 Josiah, that is, salvation of the Lord, or incense. He is the one who says: Let my prayer be directed as incense (Psalm 140), etc. Josiah, a just king; his sons whom he begot were not in the transmigration, since he never was transported, but according to God's predestination they were to be transported; the evangelist places Jechoniah and his brothers together, so that those whose iniquity is common might have a like misery. Jechoniah, preparation of the Lord, because the Lord prepared both father and son for transportation. ISIDORE. The truth of the history is that there were two Jechoniahs, so that one is the father at the end of the preceding set of fourteen, the other at the beginning of the following. But mystically, according to Augustine, one and the same is in the faith of the preceding and at the beginning of the following. But why was Jehoiakim, the father of Jechoniah, passed over? Perhaps so that he might make a type of Christ, he counted Jechoniah twice, and passed over Jehoiakim lest the number be increased. All who are counted from David to the Babylonian transmigration were kings. Jechoniah. The first Jechoniah is called the resurrection of the Lord, the next Jechoniah the preparation of the Lord. Both suit Christ, who is the resurrection and the life (John 11).
1.12: 1.12 Shealtiel. My petition, God; this suits Christ, who says: Holy Father, keep those whom you have given me, that they may be one as we also are (John 17).
1.13: 1.13 And Zerubbabel begot Abiud. Master of Babylon, that is, of confusion. It suits him who called the world back from the error of idolatry to the way of truth. There were zealous men among the Jews, called Heriles because of their nearness to the family of Christ, and they were Nazarenes; they wrote down the order of Christ's genealogy, keeping it partly from memory, partly from the books of Chronicles, partly from grandfathers and great-grandfathers, according to the order. Abiud, that is, my father. This suits Christ, of whom it is said: He has called upon me: You are my father (Psalm 88), etc. Eliakim. The Lord raising up. He is the one who says: Everyone who sees the Son and believes in him will have eternal life, and I will raise him up (John 6), etc.
1.14: 1.14 Azor. Helped. He is the one who says: Behold, God helps me, the Lord is the protector of my soul (Psalm 53). Zadok. Just, that is, Christ, of whom it is said: The Lord is just and has loved justice (Psalm 10). Achim, that is, this my brother. Who else but he who willed to become man, that he might have brothers, of whom he would say: I will declare your name to my brothers (Psalm 21). Eliud, that is, my God, suits Christ, who says: My God, why have you forsaken me? (Matthew 27).
1.15: 1.15 Eleazar, that is, my God, helper. He is the one who in the person of man said: My God, I will hope in him (Psalm 90). Matthan. Giving, or given. He is the one who gave good things to men, and of whom it is said: God so loved the world that he gave his Son (John 3). Through these fathers Christ came into the world, and he bore in himself the office of all of them. And it is fitting that we ascend to him by the same line of holiness by which he deigned to descend to us.
1.16: 1.16 Joseph. Adding; Christ, who added the Gentiles to the Jews. He is also called the father of Christ, whom he received by adoption as born of his wife; but he is also called father by supposition. Matthew calls Joseph the son of Jacob, and Jacob the son of Matthan. Luke calls Joseph the son of Heli, and Heli the son of Matthat; but Matthan and Matthat each begot a son by the same wife, Esta by name. Matthan, who descended through Solomon, married her first, and died leaving one son, Jacob; afterwards Matthat, who descended from David through Nathan, married the same woman and begot Heli; so Jacob and Heli are uterine brothers. Jacob then took the wife of his brother Heli, who had died without children, to raise up seed for him, and begot Joseph, his own son by nature but according to the law the son of Heli. The statement that the child is called by the name of the one for whom seed is raised is not true, since Boaz called the son he begot of Ruth not by the name of Elimelech, for whom seed was being raised, but Obed. The husband of Mary. What does the generation traced from David down to Joseph have to do with Christ, since Christ is not of the seed of Joseph? But it is not the custom of the Scriptures to weave the order of women into genealogies; and therefore the line is brought down not through Mary but through Joseph, since Joseph and Mary were of one tribe. Hence he was also obliged to take her as a kinswoman, lest a tribe be confused with another; hence also they went together, as being of one stock, to be registered, returning to Bethlehem, each to his own city. From the example of Mary it is clear to married believers that, by keeping equal consent, continence can remain, and that marriage is called such not by mingling of the bodily sexes but by preserving the affection of the mind. Hence Joseph is also called the husband of Mary, because marriage is true where the effect of love is preserved, and in Mary the fruit of marriage is found.
5.27: 5.27 You have heard. RABANUS. He who has said: I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill (Mark 11), adds how far it ought to abound, etc., up to: when the soul, having left the higher law, is corrupted, prostituted by the base will of the lower things. Shall see a woman. BEDE. A great addition. Sight is put for every motion which is, etc., up to: because one is accused or defended not according to what he was able to do and was not allowed, but according to what he wished and proposed from conscience. To lust after her. So that it passes into the affection of the heart, so that he disposes to do it, where it is not the will that is lacking but the occasion; which is called passion, which is death in the house. Propassion is a sudden affection of the mind, whether of anger or of love. Passion is the form or deliberation of the mind from consent. Hence someone is called irascible or a lover. ISIDORE. If contemplation turns into weariness or arrogance, leave it, and pass to the active life, because it is better to be saved by the active than to perish by the contemplative.
5.29: 5.29 Pluck it out. According to the letter no member is commanded to be plucked out, but the interior sight, which is called the right, and the exterior, which is called the left, if it harms, is to be recalled or removed by the zeal of pious labor, and even put far away, so that it is not even held in memory. The eye is plucked out when evil use is broken. It is cast away when it is wholly annihilated and not allowed to enter.
5.30: 5.30 Your right hand. Prosperous working, or some strenuous helper within the affairs of life: if he is a scandal in the law of God, it is better to be saved with him cut off than to be damned with him. Cut it off, etc. If anyone preaches this about bodily members, he ought not to be heard in the spirit of piety. But that the wickedness of morals and the depravity of actions may be cut away from it, so that whatever in the eye of the mind subverts us from the way of righteousness and uprightness of morals, and whatever outside strikes against the working of virtues, may be driven far away. Into hell. The name of gehenna is not found in the ancients, but is first set down by the Lord. The occasion of the name is this. There was an idol of Baal near Jerusalem at the foot of Mount Moriah, where Siloe was. This valley was well watered and wooded and full of delights, and a place in it was consecrated to idols; and the people of Israel went so mad that, leaving the temple, they sacrificed there and burned their sons to demons. And this place was called Gehennon, that is, the valley of Ennon. But God threatens that he will fill that place with corpses, so that it be called polyandrion, that is, a burial-place of the dead; by the name of this place, therefore, future punishments are designated.
5.31: 5.31 Let him give her. AUGUSTINE. Moses wrote in Deuteronomy that if a wife does not please her husband on account of some uncleanness, he may send her away. Which Christ explains, etc., up to: as he loves his enemy, not in that he is an enemy and wicked, but in that he is a man, so that he may be saved with him. CHRYSOSTOM. Moses permitted a bill of divorce to be given, lest blood be shed because of hatred. He permitted evils to be done, etc., up to: because we cannot fully prohibit the evil wills of men.
5.32: 5.32 Excepting for the cause of fornication. Because in this the faith of chastity and of marriage is broken; and he does not make her commit adultery, but she herself is the cause of her guilt. But if he puts her away for fornication, he ought to be free from fornication, nor is it lawful to take another while she lives. For the cause of fornication. Of the woman who has fornicated, or of the husband lest he fornicate, namely if the wife compels him to idolatry, or to avarice, or to other unlawful lusts. For fornication is not only of debauchery, but generally whatever makes one stray from the law of God. And whoever, etc. CHRYSOSTOM. Do not say that her husband put her away, since even after she is put away she remains the wife of the one who put her away.
5.33: 5.33 But you shall perform. If it happens that you swear, you shall swear by the Creator, not by a creature. For that by which one swears he venerates: he loves it, he fears it. Therefore the law commands that one swear only by God. But I, etc. He teaches that nothing among creatures is so vile that one ought to commit perjury by it, since from the highest to the lowest he forbids the oath, that is, from heaven to a hair. One is convicted of perjuring against God, whose throne is heaven and who owns whatever exists. By heaven. They either suspected something more in heaven, or those swearing by it did not think themselves bound by the oath; therefore he so tempers the sentence that heaven is believed to be a creature of God, nothing more; and because it is his throne, perjury is to be feared. So also of the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet. He, therefore, who swears by a creature owes the oath to him who created and rules it, and it is not rightly thought to be rendered to another. Let us not swear by creatures in order to venerate them beyond what we ought, nor by them so as to esteem them cheap, namely that when we swear by them we think we swear nothing. Neither by the earth. Others swear by the safety of Pharaoh, who was placed by God's judgment in the lowest place. There is no power but from God (Romans 13); and in this you swear by God. Neither, etc. Because it is not your work but God's; and so in the least things by swearing you can incur perjury. He who swears by his head owes the oath to him whose figure and power remain in it.
5.36: 5.36 Because you cannot, etc. Since these aforesaid things are arduous and difficult, no one keeps them without the spirit of fortitude. He compels to perfection when he takes away the occasion of swearing.
5.37: 5.37 Yes, yes; no, no. He says it twice so that what you say with the mouth you may prove by works. What you deny in words, do not by deeds approve or confirm. He did not forbid swearing altogether, but the occasion of perjury. He taught what is more perfect, showing that it is further to be free from evil. The Apostle swears to persuade faith; the Church even allows her members to swear for the pact of peace and faith. But Christ taught what is more perfect, what he indulged to weakness, what he cut away as superstitious. The truth of the Gospel does not receive an oath, but another's weakness compels it, when he does not believe the truth. It is of evil. Not indeed evil, for although not good it is necessary, but it is of evil, not yours but of him by whom you are compelled to swear, that is, of his weakness, which is evil.
5.38: 5.38 You have heard. AUGUSTINE. The law set a measure of vengeance: an eye for an eye. If it can be said, etc., up to: but out of love of righteousness, the just for the unjust, which is good for evil, which a judge also does. When he says, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, he does not wish to take away one, but to preserve both, while he threatens retaliation. Which he also does with measure, so that vengeance does not exceed the injury; and this is the beginning of peace and, as it were, the start of righteousness.
5.39: 5.39 Not to resist. The righteousness of the law instructs the unlearned at the beginning of righteousness, that is, to render no more than what was inflicted. The righteousness of the Gospel (which leads men to the kingdom) is not to resist evil. Not to resist: as he himself: Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart (Matthew 11). And David: If I have repaid those who did evil to me (Psalm 7). Jeremiah: And I gave my cheek to the one striking (Lamentations 3). Behold, the same Lord of the law and the Gospel. Offer him. Not only do not strike back, but if he wishes to strike the other, bear it patiently: this concerns injury to the body. But concerning necessities, if you lose one, let the rest be taken too. What then about superfluities? The other. CHRYSOSTOM. First, it is an unworthy thing that a believing man stand in judgment before the face of an unbelieving judge. For even if an unbeliever, etc., up to: If once you have entered into judgment, you no longer desire that the truth of the case appear, but that you somehow come out the victor.
5.40: 5.40 And to him that, etc. It is a counsel before you contend. It is indeed permitted to the weak to demand back their own, but not to contend. Luke conversely: Him that takes away your garment, forbid not to take your coat also. This is to be done not in these things only but in all temporal things. Your coat. Or, the coat is the soul, which if anyone is unwilling to lose, let him give up the cloak, that is, the body, to martyrdom. Spiritually, the teacher takes the coat when he makes interior vices be confessed, such as envy, pride, and the like. He adds: And the cloak, who is not ashamed to confess exterior ones also, such as theft and fornication.
5.41: 5.41 A thousand paces. This is a Sabbath day's journey, by which spiritual perfection is designated, because it is not lawful on the Sabbath to do servile work. Other two. He goes also other two who, while he is reduced to servitude in body only, is prepared to be reduced in spirit and soul, that is, in reason and will.
5.42: 5.42 Give to him. What can be given honestly and justly. If the means are lacking, give goodwill by word or service. Give to him. So, namely, that it harm neither you nor another: for righteousness is to be weighed. For thus you will give to everyone who asks, even if not what he asks, but something better when you have corrected one who asks unjustly. And to him that would. He embraces two kinds of giving. For either we give out of goodwill, or we lend to one who will repay. And sometimes he who gives does not wish to lend, as though there were no reward in it when the debtor pays back what he received. But he truly repays who commands even this. He says therefore: Turn not away, that is, do not alienate your will. For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9); so also the spiritual teacher of the divine word ought to lend to his hearers on interest, so that he may receive from them the return of good work and hope for reward from God.
5.43: 5.43 You have heard. He who came to fulfill the law leads in the end to full charity, which is the fulfillment of the law. You shall hate. Perhaps this is to be understood in line with what was said above: An eye for an eye, etc. Or by withdrawing the offices of humanity.
5.44: 5.44 Love. The Church is fought against in three ways: by hatred, by words, by torture of the body. The Church on the contrary loves, does good, prays. This is the new commandment; this makes sons of God out of sons of wrath; hence follows: That you may be sons. The adoption of sons is acquired by charity alone. Do good. By ministering food of the mind or of the body. Which he also does who says that such a one takes not even food. For all these things look to this, that they may become brothers. To each is opposed each, so that all parts of malice may be conquered by goodness. The imprecations of the prophets seem to be contrary, which are spoken not by the wish of those desiring but by the spirit of those foreseeing. Pray. AUGUSTINE. He does not say this for brothers in whom there are sometimes sins graver than the persecution of enemies, etc., up to: since even if they confess that they sinned, and repent greatly of having done evil, they nevertheless have such affections of mind that they do not humble themselves to ask pardon. But it may give pause that John in his Epistle seems to admonish only that we love the brethren concerning the love of God and neighbor, whereas the Lord says we must also pray for enemies. But brethren are understood to be not only those who already believe but those who are going to believe, for whom we must pray, that they may be joined to us in fraternal covenant.
5.45: 5.45 Sons. Not degenerate. As if he said: Having received power, act by works so that you may be sons by being reborn through charity. Of your Father. He is now called Father. See that you be sons reborn of God, who is charity. Who makes his sun. This visible one. For they say in the book of Solomon: The sun of justice has not shone upon us (Wisdom 5). And of the rain of doctrine the prophet says: I rained upon one city, and upon another I did not rain. His sun (Amos 4), etc. As if he said: He made it, and properly all things are his which he created from nothing. What then shall we do with the things we have received from his gift?
5.46: 5.46 Publicans. The tax-collectors of the Romans, whom the Jews call so because they took care of the public affairs. They are also said to have taken the name from Publius, a Roman king, who first appointed them.
5.47: 5.47 And if you salute. If you pray only for those who are joined to you by some affinity, what more does your kindness have than that of unbelievers? It is fitting to love the brethren and to greet them humbly, but it is little.
5.48: 5.48 Perfect. In the charity of God and neighbor. The summit of perfection is to love even enemies, and to pray for them, as Christ also did.
6.1: 6.1 Take heed, etc. He who up to now commanded about mercy now commands about purity of heart by which God is seen. For if works of mercy are done not with a single intention but for the praise of men, they are not approved by God. The praise of men ought not to be sought, but to follow, so that by example it invites others. So far, about the righteousness of the Gospel, which is above the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees. Now, by what purity of heart this same righteousness ought to be fulfilled, which is kept in almsgiving and prayer. For here he does not admonish either to pray or to give alms, but in what spirit we ought to do it. For the matter here is the cleansing of the heart. With your Father. Whose glory the sons ought to seek, and refer all good things to this, that they may please him.
6.2: 6.2 When therefore, etc. From the whole to the parts, to explain which good things are not to be done for the praise of men. To sound a trumpet. Perhaps they did this to call people together, so that all might go as to a spectacle. Before you. He sounds a trumpet before himself who wishes to be praised before others, that he may appear greater than they. They have received. From God, the inspector of the heart, the punishment of deceit, of whom it is said: Depart from me, deceitful workers; for you have had my name, but you have not done my works.
6.3: 6.3 Let not know. The left hand is vices; the right, virtues. What virtue does, therefore, let not pride, or vainglory, or any vice know; but let the light of right working put to flight the darkness of sin.
6.4: 6.4 In secret. Almsgiving is done in secret when it is mingled with no darkness: the light is within, the darkness outside. He sees in secret. God's seeing is approving. And he approves only what is hidden; what is outside does not please him nor does he approve it.
6.5: 6.5 And when you pray. This saying is joined to the above. Above he had said: Take heed that you do not your justice before men; here he adds: And when you pray. He does not forbid praying, but being like hypocrites in praying. In the corners. As hiders of their prayers, and yet in the streets to be seen, and through this greater glory. Allegorically: he prays in a corner who pretends to pray in secret, and yet is angling for fame in the street. The corners of the streets are where the road is led by a crossing of the way and makes a four-way junction. For it is not wrong to be seen, but to seek to be seen. They have received. In these not only is the true reward emptied by wicked intention, but the vice of pretense and mockery against God is increased.
6.6: 6.6 But you. Understood simply, this teaches that the vain glory of the world is to be fled. But it seems rather to be commanded that, with the thought of the heart enclosed and the lips closed, one pray to God. The chamber is the secret of the heart. The door is the carnal sense through which these exterior things wickedly intrude and crowds of images clamor against those praying. It is little therefore to enter the chamber if the door lies open to importunate thoughts. But the carnal sense must be resisted, that spiritual prayer may be directed to God from the depths of the heart. The door being shut: the senses closed, lest crowds of exterior images run in. Or he calls the door the love or fear of this age. For as every good thing comes from the fear and love of God, so every evil from the love and fear of the world. These being shut, that is, removed, pray. CHRYSOSTOM. What then, you say? ought one not to pray in the Church? Indeed, very much, but with this will, that you look to that One who has the power of giving what you ask. For God everywhere looks to the intention with which you do anything. Your Father. Whom you have within through faith; hence: With me is prayer to the God of my life (Psalm 41).
6.7: 6.7 And when you are praying. As it is the mark of hypocrites to be shown and to please men, so wordiness belongs to the Gentiles, from whom it also began. For these give more effort to exercising the tongue than to cleansing the mind, so that they transfer this kind of trifling office even to bending God by prayer, thinking that as an orator bends a judge, so they can bend God. CHRYSOSTOM. If one should pray briefly, why did Luke propose a parable that one ought always to pray, etc., up to: since both Christ and Paul commanded prayers to be short but frequent, at short intervals. CASSIAN. The Fathers judge that prayers are more useful when short but very frequent, etc., up to: let us avoid by concise brevity. For they think. Thinking that God is soothed by persuasive words. Or if he is absent he is summoned, and what he does not know is taught by roundabout words.
6.8: 6.8 Be not therefore like to them. For with God one must deal not with words but with deeds, with the intention of the heart, with simple affection. When we say these things we do not teach him, but we remind ourselves at the time of prayer. For your Father knows. Why then do we speak to one who knows? Not that we may make known our will, but that we may rouse the service of pious devotion.
6.9: 6.9 Our Father. BEDE. Among the other salutary and divine admonitions with which he counsels believers, he set forth a pattern of praying, etc., up to: and these are the true worshipers, who as sons by grace worship the Father in spirit and truth. No prayer is more spiritual than that which proceeded from the mouth of the Son, who is the Truth. Our Father. Whom we serve not out of fear but out of love of the inheritance. When he is called Father, let us think of adoption, that we may repay the Father with pious affection. When it is said our, we are reminded of brotherhood, since the adoption is common to all. Let no one say my, which properly suits the Son, whose father he is by nature. Hence elsewhere: I go to my Father (John 7), specially by nature; and your, joined by grace. He is called our Father, which is common to all; let no one say my: this suits Christ alone, who is Son by nature; to others the common grace of adoption is granted. RABANUS. The noble and the rich are warned not to be proud, etc., up to: What will he deny to sons, who has already given what makes him father? AUGUSTINE. Nowhere is a precept found for the people of Israel that they should say, Our Father, or pray, etc., up to: if they did not stray from his commandments. As is that: I have begotten and exalted sons (Isaiah 1), etc. In heaven. In spiritual things, so that we may learn to hasten to the spirituality in which he dwells, and seek heavenly things from him. Hallowed be your name. The distinction of these seven petitions must be seen. For since our life is lived in time and the eternal is hoped for, the first are, etc., up to: for deliverance makes free, that is, sons, that we may say by the spirit of adoption, Abba, Father. Amen signifies that in all these petitions what is asked is undoubtedly granted by the Lord, if we do not neglect to keep the covenant of the last condition. Hence he adds: If you forgive, etc. Hallowed, etc. Here we pray for the spirit of wisdom, that we may not first differ in anything from the hallowing of the name; but let the Father's name be shown in the sons by morals and life. The name of the Father is in us, who are called sons: we ask it to be hallowed, not that he himself may be holier, but that he may work in us the increase of his hallowing: for the sanctification of the sons is attributed to his name. It is said to be hallowed in the way it is said to be glorified and magnified in us. Let it be hallowed, that is, let it be held by men to be as holy as it is; and let God be so made known to them that they think nothing holier.
6.10: 6.10 Your kingdom come. Here the spirit of understanding is asked for, by which the heart is cleansed that God may be seen. The hardness and power of the devil is shut out, and in the future more perfectly, when he shall have put down all principality and power, and the kingdom shall be delivered to God the Father. It follows fittingly that after the adoption of sons we ask for the kingdom, which is due to sons. The kingdom of God is always; but let it come, that is, be manifested to men, by whom, like light to the blind, it is not seen; which no one will be able to ignore, when the Son shall come to judge. In which the saints also will reign, as it is said: Receive the kingdom prepared for you (Matthew 25), etc. By the spirit of understanding the future kingdom is declared to those entering it, and purity of heart is attributed to it, by which God reigning there will be seen as he is, where the spirit of wisdom will fulfill the seventh sanctification of his name. In the perfection of the sixth the coming of the kingdom is requested, that we may all run to the perfect man; then, for those resting in him, may he himself be sanctified in us while we are sanctified in him. We rightly ask that his rest be sanctified in us, that sanctified in him we may rest forever, in which sanctification the peace of beatitude is made firm and full wisdom is given. Your will be done. Here the spirit of counsel is asked for, by which the will of God is sought, that it may be fulfilled by us. The will of God on earth as in heaven is ruled by the spirit of counsel. We also have need of the spirit of counsel, that the will of God may be directed in us, that we may be able to be merciful in deed. The will of God is always done; but we pray that the freedom of our choice may be joined by grace to his will, which is our sanctification and eternal life. The will of God is the keeping of his precepts. As in heaven. As in the angels, so in men. Or as in the just, so in converted sinners. Or as in Christ, so in the Church. Or as I serve the law of God with my mind, so also in the flesh. According to the spirit we are heaven, according to the flesh earth. We pray therefore that as in heaven, that is in the spirit, so on earth the will be done: that flesh and spirit be the spiritual man of whom it is said: My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God. Nor is it prayed only that we may will good things, but that the will be done in us, that we may live to you, not to ourselves. These three are had more perfectly in the future, but here meanwhile we pray in part, that afterwards they may be had more perfectly. The four that follow are the supports of the present life.
6.11: 6.11 Bread. The hunger for righteousness, that it may reach fullness, is supported by the spirit of fortitude. Therefore we pray: Give us this day our daily bread: without which we would die of hunger. Bread is the body of Christ, or the word of God, or God himself, of whom we have daily need, or who is above all substances. This is the living bread which came down from heaven (John 6), whose natural sublimity is above all substances. Our. Because Christ was made ours, and God the Father with Christ has given us all things. Therefore we pray that what is ours by gift may be given daily in effect. Supersubstantial. Or daily. Because they that eat me shall yet hunger (Ecclesiasticus 44). Here daily, in the homeland eternal. This bread ought to refresh us inwardly continually through faith and charity, because without it no one can live. Or the spiritual precepts are called bread, which are always to be practiced or kept.
6.12: 6.12 And forgive, etc. After food he asks the forgiveness of sins, that he who is fed by God may live in God and come to eternal life. When we say, Forgive us our debts, we ask for the spirit of knowledge, by which we understand our offenses, which are not understood without the spirit of knowledge. For knowledge pertains to the use of temporal things, which is a virtue in avoiding evils and seeking goods, that we may weep over our own and others' contagions and desire good things. As. Behold with what caution we are bound, in which he also bends us toward one another to mercy, and promises pardon to those who sin against him, and promises pardon to us and through us to others. We ought not to deny pardon of fault; hence: When you pray, forgive if you have anything against any man; otherwise your Father will not forgive you your sins. It is allowed to demand money back from someone, but we never justly refuse the debts of sins to one who asks pardon.
6.13: 6.13 And lead us not. But enlighten us with the spirit of knowledge, that we may know in what evils we are entangled, and we ask that tears may profit: Forgive us our debts. And lead us not, etc. Not that he himself leads, but because he forsakes and allows to go. He does not pray not to be tempted, but not to be overcome even for a little. For temptation is necessary for the crown. And lead us not, etc.: forsaking us in temptation, you would let us be overcome; although you let us be tempted, without which no one is proved. But deliver us from evil. This one petition contains as much as all the above, so that by the spirit of the fear of God all harmful things may be driven out within and without, and we may live blessedly under poverty. But deliver us. Do not let us be led into that which is not yet, and from that into which we have been led, deliver us; when this is done, nothing is to be feared, nothing remains to be prayed for. From evil, all, visible and invisible. This deliverance is necessary daily, as we do not live without evil of soul and body, but it will be completed at the end, when we shall be immortal and impassible. Thus we ascend step by step from the lowest to the highest. From evil we are freed by the spirit of fear; thence freed we desire to be poor in spirit and in goods, when we say, Lead us not into temptation. We ask for the spirit of piety, that the inner man may become gentle and mild, lest he be moved by temptation.
6.14: 6.14 For if you forgive. He laid down a rule for how we wish to be judged. Hence to those who forgive, confidence of obtaining answers before God; but to those who exact, the penalty of vengeance or damnation bites back.
6.15: 6.15 But if you do not forgive. No excuse is left, because each will be judged in the future according to this sentence. From this it is plain that each is condemned in his own unfaithfulness.
6.16: 6.16 When you fast. After he taught how one must pray, he teaches about fasting, which again pertains to purity of heart, lest it be not simple toward God while it is carried off to exterior things. Be not. He does not forbid virtue, but a feigned appearance of virtue. It is good to be sad in fasting for sins, for repentance, and to humble our soul; hence: A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise (Psalm 50). But he forbids the sadness that is for praise. Hence he does not simply say: Do not fast, but adds: as the hypocrites, sad. They disfigure. That is, they draw out beyond the bounds of the human condition. As there is boasting about the splendor of garments, so about excessive squalor and leanness. To demolish is as it were to scatter, and to reduce the beauty of the face as it were to nothing. Their faces. With mournful filth in which there is also boasting; and they deceive the more under the appearance of religion. Note that sheep ought not to put off their skins, but be clothed, if at any time wolves cover themselves with them.
6.17: 6.17 Anoint your head. Refresh the mind with spiritual joy on days of abstinence, that the odor of love may be fragrant in works of mercy. Wash the conscience with tears, that it may be clean before God. For the work of mercy is not enough without a clean conscience, nor this without that. It was the custom of the Palestinians to anoint the head on feasts; therefore anoint your head, that is, show yourself festive and cheerful, and refresh the mind with spiritual oil, and do not seek praise from outside for fasting. But because you are thus turned away from the world, rejoice before God; and so you will cleanse your face, that is, your heart, of filth; which being removed, it will be allowed to see God. Anoint your head. Behold, not yet everything in the New Testament is to be taken to the letter. For they would be ridiculous, smeared with oil in fasting; but for the spirit of his love, in whose sufferings we ought to share by wasting ourselves, the mind ought to be anointed and not with the oil of flattery; otherwise fasts are vain. Christ was made ointment for us, which, poured out through the passion of death, filled his Church with its fragrance. Therefore we ought not to fast for the sake of another, but, steeped in his spirit, wasting the flesh by abstinence, let us share in his passion. Let us then be anointed with him, that works of mercy may be heaped up and charity poured within; for without him the cup of our fasting is not made drunk with the affection of piety. He fasts for God who wastes himself for love of him and gives to another what he withdraws from himself.
6.18: 6.18 And your Father. The Father is within through faith, and rewards what is done in secret. There, therefore, one must fast where he himself sees. And it is necessary that the one fasting so fast as to please him whom he carries in his heart.
6.19: 6.19 Lay not up. For the purity of heart he commands earthly things to be given out.
6.20: 6.20 But lay up. As if: when you fast or do any good work, store it where corruption cannot come. In heaven. That is, put all hope in heavenly things, walking by faith, embracing charity. In heaven, that is, in the spiritual firmament, which does not pass away: Heaven and earth shall pass away; but my words shall not pass away. If therefore the heart is in heaven, it is clean, because heavenly things are clean. But if it wallows on earth, how is it clean? That is, if one acts to obtain earthly things, how is it clean? For even those things, though clean in their kind, are soiled, the worthier thing being mixed with the lower: as gold with silver, silver with lead.
6.21: 6.21 For where your treasure is. If on earth, the heart is downward; if in heavenly things, the heart is fixed in Christ.
6.22: 6.22 The lamp. He pursues purity of heart. As the eye directs the members to work, so intention and the light of faith direct all the virtues. The lamp is a light in an earthen vessel, so charity in faith. When faith shall cease, charity alone will be light. From the exterior he teaches the office of the interior man; by the intention of the mind and the light of faith all virtues are illumined, that they may make the body bright. Likewise this chapter is for the purity of heart in itself, or for the sake of the former works which appear openly. If your eye be, etc. If with pure intention you do what good you can, the works are works of light, even if it does not so appear to men. If the intention is perverse, whatever is done is crooked, even if it seems right. The eye is single and simple, namely charity, which now shines in faith as in an earthen vessel.
6.23: 6.23 But if your eye. If the intention is not from faith, the whole interior man is dark. Because what is not of faith is sin. It will be dark. Since the intention informs the work that follows. Therefore if the good things you do are darkness because they are done with evil intention, what of those which are evil in themselves and are done with evil intention? If therefore the light. The intention with which we do anything, which is known in us, is called light; but the outcome of the matter is uncertain, as when I give or do something to someone and do not know whether it turns out to his good or evil; and so he calls it darkness. He says therefore: If the intention with which you act (which is known to you) is soiled by appetite for temporal things, how much more the deed itself, whose outcome is doubtful? For even if it turns out well for another, what you do without good intention will profit you nothing, because it is counted to you how you did it, not how it turned out for him.
6.24: 6.24 No man can, etc. As if: you cannot do good things before the eyes of men and from these please God. Nor lay up treasure in heaven and on earth at once, nor serve both vices and virtues. Whatever you do is either from love of God or in servitude to the devil. Since the kingdom of God and of the devil are at variance with each other, no one can serve in both at once; hence those who are baptized renounce the devil and his works. For either he will hate the one. There is nothing in between. For whatever you do, it is either from love of God or from servitude to the devil. AUGUSTINE. The devil must always be held in hatred; but God, etc., up to: but they despise, conquered by their own concupiscence and the devil's persuasion. Or he will sustain the one. The same. He does not indeed love: for no one loves the devil; but entangled by his own cupidity, etc., up to: even if he does not love him whose handmaid he loves. And despise the other. He will not indeed hate: for no one's conscience can hate God, which the same Augustine retracted, saying: I do not see that it should have been said. For there are many of whom it is written: The pride of them that hate you (Psalm 3), etc. And mammon. Mammon, in the Syrian tongue, riches, to serve which is to deny God. He does not say to have, which can be done so as to dispense well, but to serve, which is of the avaricious. This name is said to be that of the demon who presides over riches, not because they are in his dominion, but because he uses them to deceive, ensnaring with the snares of riches.
6.25: 6.25 Therefore I say to you, etc. Because you cannot serve God and mammon. Be not solicitous, which is to serve riches. Throughout the whole discourse he commanded contempt of the world and trust in the things to come, when he ordered to endure evils and not to avenge, and to love enemies, and to flee human glory. Now he wishes to confirm through faith in the hope of eternal things, because there are many whom love of present things and despair of future ones make sluggish. In the sweat of the face bread is prepared, but labor is to be exercised, and solicitude removed, which disturbs the mind while it fears lest possessions perish or what is toiled for not be obtained. For your life. That is, your animal nature, to which these things are necessary. Commit all hope to God, because you can acquire or retain nothing except what he has decreed. Soul (anima) is here put for life, which is sustained by food, as there: He that loves his life shall lose it (John 12). The animal nature is nourished by food, and is here put for life: it lives with the cattle. Whoever loses it for Christ will find it spiritual unto eternal life. Is not the life more than the meat? etc. Not life for the sake of food, nor body for the sake of clothing, but the opposite. Therefore let the mind not be solicitous to obtain what was created for its sake. As if he said: He who gave the greater things, that is life and body, will give also the lesser, that is food and clothing. In these promises of truth let no one doubt: let man be what he ought to be, and soon all things are added to him for whose sake they were made.
6.26: 6.26 Behold. This is about food. The saints are rightly compared to birds, because they seek heaven, and some are so removed from the world that they now do nothing on earth but by contemplation alone already dwell in heaven. Of whom it is said: Who are these that fly as clouds? (Isaiah 60), etc. These examples do not forbid providence from laboring, but solicitude, so that all your trust may be in God, since even birds live without care. And your Father. He magnifies and confirms the trust of the sons: for if the Father's goodness extends even to those, how much more to sons of adoption?
6.27: 6.27 And which of you, etc. But leave the care of ruling the body to him who made it reach this measure.
6.28: 6.28 And for clothing. Not that it is unbecoming to labor and provide for this, but all solicitude is to be cast off, and hope is to be held in God. Consider the lilies of the field. He confirms the exhortation about clothing with a fitting example.
6.29: 6.29 For neither Solomon, etc. What purple of kings, what embroidery of weavers can be compared to flowers? The very color is called the covering of flowers, as we say: a blush covered him.
6.30: 6.30 And if the grass of the field. If God adorns so beautifully these things, which are for the use of a time only and, soon to fall, will be burned in the fire. Tomorrow is put for the future in the Scriptures, as Jacob says: My righteousness shall answer for me tomorrow (Genesis 30). Is cast into the oven. Other books have: into the fire, or into a heap which has the appearance of an oven. How much more you, namely, will he clothe; and therefore all trust is to be had in him; for if we are not confident even about these things, how do we hope for invisible ones? It is a very small faith that is not sure even about the least things. So he instills trust also about eternal things, and condemns unbelief. O you of little faith. Whoever doubts in any promise is of little faith, and the more he doubts, the less he finds of those things for which he was anxious.
6.31: 6.31 Be not therefore solicitous, etc. He more fully inculcates and revolves what he taught from the beginning of the discourse, that we live without solicitude. Be not, etc. Here those seem to be rebuked who, having despised common food or clothing, seek for themselves more refined or more austere food or clothing than those with whom they live. To be solicitous. Solicitude chokes the word of God, that it bear no fruit, and makes one like the Gentile, that is, the unbeliever.
6.32: 6.32 For all these things. What more then does he have than the Gentile, whose unbelief troubles the mind and wearies it with the cares of this life? The Gentiles. Who have no care for the future, but it is for sons to seek the kingdom. For he knows. These things are provided by God, who knows that they are necessary for us on his way. Your Father. Thus he makes his sons secure, without care, about the goodness and providence of the Father.
6.33: 6.33 Seek therefore. Here he openly shows that these things are not to be sought as our goods, even if necessary. But the kingdom of God is to be sought, and in it our end is to be placed, for the sake of which we do all things: for example, let us eat in order to preach the Gospel, not preach the Gospel in order to eat. When he says first, he signifies this latter not in time but in dignity. For that is to be sought, and this is necessary for that; therefore seek first the kingdom of God, that is, put it before all other things. And all these things. Because all things are the sons': and therefore all these things shall be added, even to those not seeking them; if they are withdrawn, it is for testing; if given, for thanksgiving; because all things work together for good.
6.34: 6.34 Solicitous. With fear, grief, and the anxiety of cares which disturb the mind. For tomorrow. AUGUSTINE. He concedes concern for the future regarding present things; hence the Apostle: Night and day we worked, that we might not burden any of you (1 Thessalonians 2). It is not fitting, about future things which the divine ordering provides, etc., up to: because he who commanded this, whom angels served, had a purse for the sake of giving this example, so that he might supply what was necessary for uses, of which Judas was the keeper. The day. Not that which the Lord made, but that which Job and Jeremiah cursed, namely that which the devil finds. Sufficient. And because minds are overwhelmed by present care, the malice of God ought not to be made to sprout.
7.1: 7.1 Judge not. About doubtful matters, because judgment is made on manifest things and not on those of which it is uncertain in what spirit they are done, about which no one judges without danger. Judgment is rash when those to whom it has not been committed judge, whether it concerns manifest or hidden things. Judgment is committed either to the masters of the Church or to the rulers of the earth. If these, therefore, judge about manifest things, namely those which are convicted or confessed, they do not judge rashly; but if about uncertain things, they judge rashly, and he forbids such judgments.
7.2: 7.2 For with what. As if he said: In whatever will you have done good, in that you will be freed; and in whatever evil, in that same you will be punished. For the matter concerns those things in which by rash judging we offend, or by acting rightly we are excused; and so he adds: With what measure. And justly, those whose will had no end of sinning, although they sinned with an end, have no end of punishment; and those whose judgment was without mercy will be judged without mercy. With what measure. It can be that in this measure in which one thing is measured, such as wheat, another is measured, such as barley; and another quantity, as if one bushel from one, a hundred from another. So God does, and not unjustly, as those do in eternity. And the very infamy, or the evil you have borne, is the cause why you incur the penalty due. Justly, those who wish to enjoy sin eternally find also eternal punishment: those whose will had no end of sinning will have no end of torment.
7.3: 7.3 And why do you see. Behold the moderation of judgment: let him who is beset by greater faults not judge another about lesser ones. For many, beset by greater faults, want more to blame and condemn lighter ones in a brother than to amend them. As when, full of hatred or envy or malice, they condemn in him what anger commits; anger is like the mote, hatred like the beam. One who is angry at someone sometimes wishes him to be corrected; one who hates cannot wish this; and so it is called impossible for one who bears a beam to take the mote from his brother. First, therefore, the beam of hatred, envy, pretense and all malice must be cast out, so that we can thus rebuke a brother mercifully, with regard to God, not ourselves, that whether the correction benefits him or not, we may yet be secure from the simplicity of our own eye. Scarcely anyone is found free from this vice, because each, favoring his own, easily reproves others' faults; and, bearing others' more heavily than his own, takes authority to rebuke without the example of his own amendment.
