In that they judge rashly they have a beam in the eye, to their own harm.
7.4: 7.4 Or how do you say to your brother. That is, you will not be able to amend the lesser thing (such as anger) in a brother until you have driven the greater, that is, hatred or envy, from your heart.
7.5: 7.5 Hypocrite, cast out. For these undertake to accuse everything out of hatred and spite, and wish to appear as counselors without the example of their own amendment. For one is not a fit teacher to heal another who has not yet healed himself.
7.6: 7.6 Give not that which is holy, etc. With the eye purged, the dispensers of the Church can chastise others, but not give what is holy to dogs; for as it is dangerous to hide it, so it is wasteful to give it to dogs. To such the mystical things are not to be opened, but the holies of holies are to be covered with a veil; the plainer and as it were cheaper things may be spoken. Give not. The same thing is called holy and pearl, that is, the Gospel and the sacraments of the Church. Holy, because by nature inviolable, nor should it be corrupted by anyone. Pearl, which lies hidden in secret, and from figures, as from opened shells, is drawn out, is a precious gem which cannot be corrupted. Dogs truly are those who bark against it and tear to pieces what is whole; swine, those who despise and trample; or dogs returned to their vomit, swine not yet converted but wallowing in the mud of vices. And turning. Lest perhaps they burst out while still hearing something, not against the pearls which they trample, but against you in indignation. For it cannot easily be found what would be pleasing to such.
7.7: 7.7 Ask. By these steps the way, the truth, and the life are granted to those who strive lawfully: Christ is the way by which one walks, the truth by which he is found, the door at which one knocks, that through him we may enter to him. AUGUSTINE. I thought it needful to explain at length how these three differ among themselves, but far better, etc., up to: for he did not say, to those asking, and seeking, and knocking.
7.8: 7.8 For every one, etc. To afford constancy in persevering, diligence in seeking, confidence in obtaining, he adds. Every one, etc. Above he taught what we should ask, namely the kingdom. Here confidence, that we ask with no hesitation. He who of his own accord offered himself to those not asking does not deny himself to those asking; and those seeking will find him who gave to those not seeking that they might find; and to those knocking he will open, who cries: Behold, I stand at the door and knock (Apocalypse 3).
7.9: 7.9 Or what man. He explains what is to be asked, and from human kindness toward children commends the Father's diligence toward us. To those asking for Christ in right faith, a stone of offense and hardness of heart is not given. So if you ask your Father for charity, without which the rest are nothing, as a table is poor without bread, to which hardness of heart is contrary.
7.10: 7.10 Or a fish. By the fish, the faith that is nourished under the streams of the Holy Spirit. He calls the fish the faith in invisible things: either because of the water of baptism, or because it is caught from invisible places, or because it is not broken by the waves of this world. In the Gospel of Luke there follows the comparison of the egg and the scorpion. In the egg hope is understood, because in it the offspring is not yet developed, but by cherishing it is hoped for. In the scorpion, whose sting is to be feared from behind, is understood the contrary of hope, namely to look back, since hope ought to stretch itself forward.
7.11: 7.11 If you then. Since fathers give good things to their children, much more will our Father, who is incomparably good, give good things to the children who ask him. You know to give good gifts. Good according to the sense of those who hold them as good, although they are also good in the nature of things, and pertain to this life, which the wicked does not give of his own. For the earth is the Lord's (Psalm 23), etc. Or the apostles are called evil as to themselves, in respect of God, who alone is good, from whom all are good. He will give good things. That is, the Holy Spirit. Or good things, namely eternal, which are given only to sons. To them that ask him. The distributor of all spiritual goods, that the works of charity may be fulfilled.
7.12: 7.12 All things therefore, etc. Because to love one who loves is of nature; but to be compelled by benefits to love one who does not love is of the perfection of Christ. Since he commanded that we, going first, do to others what we wish done to us, he soon adds the same sense, saying: All things therefore whatsoever, etc., that is, the good things which you wish to receive from others, do the same to them, that charity of neighbor may be fulfilled, which without love cannot rightly be perfected. And so he adds: This is the law and the prophets, etc.; because neither is God loved without neighbor nor neighbor without God, because the neighbor is not to be judged out of hatred or envy: therefore in the charity with which you would wish to be admonished, do to others. That men should do to you. Because he adds, men, he speaks only of love of neighbor. Hence he does not add, the whole law, but leaves out love of God. For if he had said: All things whatsoever you wish done to you, do to others, he would have embraced both, in which the whole law, written for the salvation of men, is in the prophets and the law.
7.13: 7.13 Enter ye in. Even if it is hard to do to others what you wish done to yourself, it must nevertheless be done so that we may enter. By the narrow gate. The narrow one is sought, and not found by all. Nor do all who find it enter by it, because those captured by the world turn back. And broad. Even if they do not seek it, all find it, because they are born in it. Pleasure, like an importunate harlot, invites all with her delights; and so many enter by it.
7.14: 7.14 How narrow. It is narrow enough to pass over everything, to love one thing only, to seek one thing, to knock daily at one, not to court prosperity, not to fear adversity. And few. If few find it, fewer strive to enter by it. No one enters without labor and without purity of mind.
7.15: 7.15 Beware. When he had said that the narrow way is found by few, lest his hearers be entangled in the errors of false prophets, he added: Beware. What he said above of the broad gate he says more openly of false prophets. Beware. Although this can be taken of all who show one thing in habit and speech, another in work, yet especially of heretics who, covered with a certain garment of piety, are ravening wolves with a venomous mind and intent to harm, either outwardly, if opportunity is given, by persecuting, or inwardly by corrupting. Who come to you in the clothing of sheep. In the sight of men they are like ministers of righteousness while they fast, pray, give alms; but these are not their fruits, because it is reckoned to them as a vice. By their fruits. JEROME. Not by the garment but by works; which of the manifest, etc., up to: but sheep ought not to put off their skins, even if wolves sometimes cover themselves with them.
7.16: 7.16 Do men gather. Allegorically: thorns and thistles are heretics, from whom none of the wise can find holiness or truth, but they tear and make bloody those who approach. Or thorns and thistles are the cares of the world and the stings of vices. Grapes and figs are the sweetness of new conduct which Christ hungers for in us, and the fervor of love which gladdens the heart of man. Therefore grapes and figs are not from thorns and thistles: because a mind still pressed by the habit of the old man can pretend not to bear the fruits of the new man. But if at times the words or deeds of the wicked profit the good, the wicked do not do this, but it is done from them by the counsel of God: for it is not their fruit but the vine which sometimes abounds over thorns. But the cluster is to be plucked and the thorn avoided. The vine is Christ. His own are the branches that bear grapes, that is, the works of the spirit that intoxicate the mind.
7.17: 7.17 So every tree. That is, according to the aforesaid impossibility: because from an evil root the fruit of sweetness cannot burst forth. Good fruits are to be expected from a good tree. A tree good or bad is not nature, which in all is created good by God, but the will good or bad. Fruits, the works, which neither can be good from an evil will nor evil from a good will. The fruits of a good tree are joy, peace, patience, longanimity, etc.; which fruits only a good will brings forth. So, on the contrary, evil intention nourishes the wicked.
7.18: 7.18 Cannot. He does not say: An evil tree cannot become good, or a good tree evil; because Paul was made an apostle from a persecutor, and the soul, nature remaining whole, is corrupted by the affection of the will or changed for the better. The will of each is the good or bad tree. And as a tree is rooted in the earth, so the will in the soul. The fruits of the evil tree are the works of the flesh, namely unclean fornication, lust.
7.19: 7.19 Every tree. By this sentence he condemns hypocrites and false prophets, and confirms by this example what he taught above about purity of heart: that no one gathers good fruit from an evil intention, nor reaps from a good one anything but good.
7.20: 7.20 Therefore by their fruits. As if he said: Beware of false prophets, and know them by their fruits.
7.21: 7.21 Not every one that says. As those are to be avoided who have the appearance of a good life for the sake of a wicked doctrine, so here, on the contrary, those who, being of sound faith and doctrine, live shamefully. For both are necessary, that the work be proved by speech and speech by works. He that says: Lord, Lord. The way of the kingdom of God is obedience, not the calling of the name. It is not truly and properly to say this where the utterance is at odds with the will. Of which the Apostle says: No man can say, The Lord Jesus, but by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12).
7.22: 7.22 Many will say. But one must especially beware of those who, in the name of Christ, even have miracles; although the Lord did these on account of unbelievers, he nevertheless warned that we not be deceived by such, thinking that invisible wisdom is there where a visible miracle is; hence he adds: Many will say. How pure and simple an eye is needed, then, to find the way of wisdom amid so many deceptions.
7.23: 7.23 I never knew you. The light does not know darkness, that is, does not look at it, because if it looked, there would be no darkness. You that work iniquity. Not you who have worked, lest it take away repentance, but you who are in the judgment; although you do not have the ability to sin, you nevertheless have the desire.
7.24: 7.24 Every one therefore. As if he said: All the aforesaid things are to be held well, because he who holds them will be likened to Christ; he who does not, to the devil. But he who, the things that were held on the mountain: he says this to show that the sermon held on the mountain is perfect in all the precepts by which the Christian life is formed. He shall be likened. Because as Christ builds one Church from various persons, instructs and rules her, to dedicate her for eternal life, so this man builds for himself an everlasting dwelling with various virtues, and in the future dedication will rejoice with Christ. To a wise man. To him who says: As a wise architect, I have laid the foundation in Christ. Who built. He builds in Christ who does what he hears from him. Upon a rock. From which Peter received his name for the firmness of faith, that is, upon himself he built the Church.
7.25: 7.25 And the rain fell. The devil attacks in three ways: by concupiscence of the flesh, by the exterior delights of the world, or by himself, when the wind of impulses looses all. Rain. Concupiscence, by which each is tempted, which softens the sense and rigor of faith; if it does not succeed, greater rivers come.
7.26: 7.26 Everyone that hears these my words, etc., outwardly. And therefore he has no excuse, but his ruin is great: because he despised the warnings of salvation. To a foolish man. Of whom it is said: An enemy hath done this; whose works are all unstable, and ruins lie open. Upon the sand. Whatever things are founded upon the concupiscence of vices will not stand.
7.27: 7.27 And it fell, and great was the fall thereof. Every conscience that does not remain fixed in God by hope cannot hold out in temptations; and it is driven the more, the more it is separated from higher things in those that are of the world; and truly all the wicked, or the falsely good, become worse when any temptation comes upon them.
7.28: 7.28 The multitudes. Or some in the crowd, because unbelievers, or rather all, at the excellence of wisdom.
8.1: 8.1 And when he was come down. After the Lord's descent from the mountain, etc., up to: it shows after what interval of time. And when he was come down. According to Luke, he also made in a level place the sermon which perhaps he had already given above. There followed. Some out of love, some for the teaching, some for wonder and healing.
8.2: 8.2 Adored him, saying: Lord. Before he asked, he showed the worship of divinity. If you will, you can make me clean. I do not doubt about the will as one unbelieving of piety; but as conscious of my own foulness I do not presume.
8.3: 8.3 Stretching forth. After the sermon he works miracles, by which the sermon is confirmed among the hearers. He touched. Not because he could not heal without touch, but to indicate that he is not subject to the law, but the Lord of the law, who does not fear contagion. He touched. Because of humanity, to teach us to despise no one because of any bodily defilement. It appears that above the law (which excludes the leper) is grace, which heals him; as he says: I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill, etc. I will. He healed in the same way in which he had been entreated, then commands: Be made clean. Behold power.
8.4: 8.4 See you tell no man, etc. He ordered him to be silent, and yet he could not be silent. Not that he wished something and was not able, but he gives an example, that his own, in the great things they do, may wish to lie hidden; but that they may profit others, they are made known against their will. Tell no man (Mark 1). Yet this one, Mark, where he says that he preached this, as though he had become an Evangelist. Go. He sends him to the priests out of humility, to show honor to the priests to whom the law commands the cleansed to offer gifts, and that seeing they may believe him; or if they do not believe, they may be without excuse, and lest he seem to break the law. Show yourself to the priest. That the priest may understand that he has been cured not by the order of the law but by the grace of God above the law. Offer, etc. Because I do not destroy the law, because the true sacrifice has not yet begun. For a testimony. That is, let them believe the Lord, if the leprosy of impiety departs. For a testimony. Of spiritual healing; the spiritual gift to be offered is man himself.
8.7: 8.7 I will come and heal him. And the centurion answering said, etc. Great humility, etc., up to: lest through lack of bodily strength he be thought to go in the body.
8.8: 8.8 I am not worthy. Because of the awareness of a Gentile life, he fears more to be burdened by the presence than helped, because although he was endowed with faith, he was not yet imbued with the sacraments. But what our weakness does not presume, grace knows how to give.
8.9: 8.9 For I also, etc. If I, a man, etc., up to: as Cornelius is called a just man and one fearing God (Acts 10).
8.11: 8.11 From the east and the west they shall come and shall sit down. Or the east are those who, once enlightened, pass over at once; the west, those who endure sufferings to death. By these two parts of the world are designated those from which the Gentiles were to be called.
8.12: 8.12 But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out. Because in this world they enjoy the benefits of God, according to that: He rains upon the just and the unjust. Now they are seen in the face of the Lord, but then not at all. Into the exterior darkness. Because they will be expelled outside by the Lord, etc., up to: he repents obstinately of what he did wrong. Weeping. By this the greatness of the torments is shown. By weeping, the torment of the soul; by gnashing of teeth, of the body.
8.14: 8.14 And when he was come, etc. When this was done Matthew has not expressed, etc., up to: to suggest to his memory the things to be narrated. And in a fever. Fever in Greek, in Latin fervor; and if at any time this passion makes one tremble, it belongs to human nature.
8.15: 8.15 And he touched, etc. Luke says that they asked, etc., up to: as Who understands sins? From my hidden ones cleanse me (Psalm 8). And she arose, etc. It is natural for those with fever, when health begins, to grow weary, etc., up to: she ministers in spirit.
8.16: 8.16 And when evening was come, etc. The setting of the sun is the death of Christ, through which he healed more possessed than he healed the sick before while living in the flesh.
8.18: 8.18 And Jesus seeing. It is manifest that it was another day, etc., up to: let us cross the bitter waves of the age.
8.19: 8.19 And a certain scribe coming. That Matthew says this was done when he ordered them to go across the strait, but Luke says as they were walking in the way, is not contrary, because they were walking by the way to come to the strait. Master. As though one of many. He himself was a man of letters, not a spiritual hearer. Master. He did not say, Lord, but master, thinking him one of many masters.
8.20: 8.20 The foxes have holes. As if he said: Why do you follow me for the gains of the age, etc., up to: for the divinity of Christ there is no place. But the Son of man has not, etc. Although men call him Son of God, he calls himself Son of man, for the sake of humility.
8.21: 8.21 And another. Note that this one was called by Jesus. Lord. The one who thrust himself forward calls him master, like a proud Pharisee; the other, who was received, calls him Lord humbly, like the publican.
8.22: 8.22 Their dead. Those who went out by guilt, that they themselves live with guilt. To bury the dead is to cherish sinners in sin.
8.23: 8.23 And when he was entered. He who did great things on land passes to the sea, to do them there also, and to appear Lord of land and sea.
8.24: 8.24 And behold, a great tempest. The storm did not arise of itself, but by his command, that the disciples might fear more and ask, and that he might show his power to those asking. He was asleep. The Lord sleeps in us, that is, the faith of the Lord, when we act more negligently, and therefore the tempest. But if faith rises again, it commands the winds and the waves.
8.25: 8.25 They awakened him. First, Jesus is to be roused in tribulations by prayers, that after the rebuke, rising, he may command the winds and the sea, and there be a great calm.
8.26: 8.26 Of little, etc. If you knew him mighty on land, why do you not believe also on the sea? He who believes little is rebuked; he who believes nothing is despised. He commanded, etc. He who is commanded perceives the one commanding. Note that every creature perceives its Creator. What are insensible things among us are sensible to these.
8.27: 8.27 What manner of man is this, etc. ORIGEN. What manner of man is this, greater than Moses, etc., up to: they who have no hearing obey.
8.28: 8.28 Into the country of the Gerasenes. Gerasa is a city of Arabia, etc., up to: visited by Christ through preachers. Two possessed. Mark and Luke speak of one, etc., up to: they showed the foulness of the bodies. Exceeding fierce. Mark says that no one now could bind the possessed man, etc., up to: they attack anyone who passes by.
8.29: 8.29 Jesus, Son of God. HILARY. They are to be believed to have suspected rather than known. AMBROSE. Jesus, Son of God. He made himself known to them only as much as he wished, etc., up to: they saw it in him, they did not believe. Before the time. For they knew that it was to come to them in the judgment of God, etc., up to: for there were two thousand, as Mark says. To torment us. The presence of Christ is torture to them; or they are tormented while they are cast out of the bodies in whose torture they delighted, as the presence of God is the refreshment of the angels.
8.31: 8.31 Send us. Note that they are much less able to harm men by their own power, since they cannot harm even cattle. Unless a man has lived after the manner of a swine, the devil does not receive power over him, unless perhaps for testing.
8.32: 8.32 And behold, with great. Man is worthier than beasts, since for the salvation of two men two thousand swine perished. The people of the Gentiles having been freed, unbelievers perform evil rites in hidden places, submerged in a blind and deep curiosity.
8.33: 8.33 And they that kept them fled. Because even some chiefs of the impious, though they flee the faith of Christ, yet do not cease to proclaim his power in wonder.
8.34: 8.34 Went out to meet. BEDE. Those who went out signify some bound by habit, who indeed marvel at and venerate the law of Christ, but do not wish to suffer it; hence they ask him to depart. And they found the man (as Luke says) clothed and in his right mind, sitting at the feet of Jesus (Luke 8). They besought him. They ask not out of pride but out of humility, judging themselves unworthy, as Peter did, and the widow with Elijah. They feared lest the presence of his holiness destroy them for their sins, as he had destroyed the swine.
9.1: 9.1 Into his own city. Do not think this is Nazareth, etc., up to: Capernaum as a kind of metropolis.
9.2: 9.2 They brought. They are the teachers who lift up and bring to Christ by admonishing and interceding. Their faith. How much one's own faith avails with God, with whom another's has so availed that it healed the man within and without. Be of good heart, son, your sins are forgiven you. Luke says: Man, etc., up to: removing the cause of the sickness, he afterwards cures the body.
9.5: 9.5 Which is easier. Note that infirmities sometimes happen because of sins, etc., up to: hence: The Lord will crush them with a double contrition. BEDE. Which is easier; but since you do not believe this spiritual thing, let it be proved by a visible sign, which is of no less power, so that in the Son of man you may recognize the hidden power of majesty, which can forgive sins as God.
9.6: 9.6 Then he says to the man sick of the palsy. Behold, through remission of the penalty understand the forgiveness of the fault. Arise. To arise is to draw the soul away from carnal desires. To take up the bed is to lift the flesh from earthly desires to the will of the spirit. To go into the house is to return to paradise, or to the inner guard of oneself, lest he sin again. Take up your bed and go into your house. That what was the testimony of infirmity may be the proof of health.
9.7: 9.7 And he arose. Great power, where health accompanies the command without delay. Hence rightly those who were present, leaving off blasphemies, amazed, turn to the praise of so great a majesty.
9.9: 9.9 He saw a man. Here it seems more probable that he recalls things passed over, since he chose the twelve before the sermon. At the custom house. In Greek telonion, in Latin vectigal (toll). Matthew in Hebrew, in Latin given, who received so great a gift of grace; Levi, added or taken up, because divine election took him up and added him to the number of the apostles. Matthew. The other Evangelists, out of modesty, etc., up to: the aforesaid discourse was. Rising up. BEDE. Luke says more fully: leaving all things, he followed him in body as well as in mind. Not led by levity, but by the truth of his works, and drawn by divine power working within, in perfect obedience and perfect renunciation, he left his gains, eager to follow Christ.
9.10: 9.10 In the house. He does not say whose, but Luke expresses it, etc., up to: is shown in the conversion of penitents. Behold, many publicans. A good omen: already by his example many are converted. Already he draws many after him, the future Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles. JEROME. Publicans and sinners. Tertullian says these were Gentiles, etc., up to: he commanded: Go not into the way of the Gentiles. The sinners coming sat down. The penitent, by the example of Matthew, hoping for pardon; hence Mark says here: for there were many that followed him (Mark 2).
9.11: 9.11 Why does your master eat with publicans. Every question, etc., up to: and all that he did serve salvation.
9.12: 9.12 But Jesus hearing, said. Both he strengthens in faith the penitents who have been received, and provokes the proud to the grace of humility and piety. They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill. The physician is Christ, etc., up to: those who receive the word of God cannot hunger.
9.13: 9.13 But go and learn. To those swollen with false righteousness he gives counsel of correction, etc., up to: the sheep, and the drachma, and the two sons. For I am not come to call the just. Did he not call Nathanael, and Peter, and Andrew, etc., up to: now they do not seem just to themselves.
9.14: 9.14 But your disciples do not fast. John, Mark and Luke, etc., up to: you may understand grace and power.
9.15: 9.15 Can the children. As if he said: You will do, as mourners, etc., up to: but from all earthly things. To mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them. By this word he expresses that fast, etc., up to: afterwards they will fast, they will not mourn. And then they shall fast. Mourning for the absence of the bridegroom was neither lacking in the fathers before the incarnation, nor after the passion, except as long as he conversed in the flesh with the disciples. They shall fast. From love of the world, not only from foods. For spiritual fasting, since it is part of the new life, does not yet suit those who are given in other things to the old life.
9.16: 9.16 And no man. As if he said: Carnal men not yet strengthened in the faith of the passion and resurrection, etc., up to: it does not suit the old age itself. For it takes away. That is, the perfection of the new life, which is one, is divided, and the faith which it has is taken from the old, to which the perfection of the new was owed.
9.17: 9.17 Neither do they put. He compares the same disciples to old wineskins, etc., up to: in the newness of sense we are reformed within.
9.18: 9.18 Behold a certain ruler came up. Mark and Luke call him the ruler of the synagogue, etc., up to: he began to hope and to seek a remedy.
9.20: 9.20 And behold a woman who. The Gentiles seized by sure hope the salvation prepared for the Jews. Twelve years. For twelve years she flowed, as that daughter also had grown to twelve; because from the time the Synagogue began to serve God, the Gentiles began to be defiled by idolatry and sin. She came. She believed, she said, because by these three, faith and work, all salvation is acquired.
9.21: 9.21 If I shall touch. The hem, not the garment. Because she did not see the Lord in the flesh, but received through the apostles the word of the incarnation. Blessed is he who touches even the outermost part of the word with faith.
9.22: 9.22 Be of good heart, daughter. She believed indeed who asked, but he instills strength and perseverance in faith.
9.23: 9.23 When he saw. The flute players are those singing a mournful song. These are the masters soothing their subjects with their grief, and the crowd of Jews kicking against the teaching of Christ. And the multitude. Because the Synagogue the joy of the Lord's indwelling, etc., up to: it obeyed in the reception.
9.24: 9.24 Is not. To you she is dead. But to God, who can raise up, she sleeps, as much in soul as in body.
9.25: 9.25 And when the multitude was put forth. That is, when the mockers were rejected, he entered into the minds of the elect. And took her by the hand. Unless first the hand of the Jews, etc., up to: repentance can blot out the secret things.
9.27: 9.27 As Jesus passed. That is, from the house of the ruler into your house. The ruler's house is the Synagogue, his own house the heavenly Jerusalem. Two blind men, etc. Two blind men, two peoples ignorant, etc., up to: the same deed, but another similar.
9.32: 9.32 A man. He signifies the Gentile people, or the whole race of men, who, led through preaching to Christ and idolatry being taken away, confessed Christ. In Greek it is more usual, but yet indifferently, to say both mute and deaf.
9.34: 9.34 But the Pharisees. In the Pharisees the unbelief of the Jews is signified.
10.1: 10.1 And having called together. From the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, etc., up to: the centurion's servant healed. The twelve. These are the workers who were to be sent, and who would call the parts of the four-cornered world to the faith of the Trinity. That their preaching might have the weight of authority, power is given them of curing every infirmity.
10.2: 10.2 Peter and Andrew. He joins the apostles in pairs and yokes, etc., up to: Christ in whom he believed.
10.3: 10.3 Thomas. Abyss; because he penetrated the depth of divine power in the resurrection by sure faith. Or, Thomas, twin, which in Greek is didymus, because of the doubtful heart in believing.
10.4: 10.4 And Judas Iscariot. A great example of teaching in us, that he who knew all things did not hesitate to choose a betrayer as a disciple and to ordain him an apostle. For Christ has a witness conscious of purity, since he does not hesitate to choose his own betrayer.
10.5: 10.5 Into the way. After the resurrection he says: Teach all nations. But this before: because it is fitting that it be preached first to the Jews, lest they have a reason for not receiving, because he sent the apostles to the Gentiles.
10.7: 10.7 The kingdom of heaven is at hand. Through faith the kingdom is near. For as the sinning earth, so the just man is heaven, in which God presides; hence it is said: The kingdom of God is within you (Luke 17), etc. Behold what they ought to preach: The kingdom of heaven is at hand.
10.8: 10.8 Heal the sick. The Church strengthens the sick in the state of good work, raises the dead in sins, or without faith; cleanses lepers sprinkled with errors; drives out demons by exorcisms. Freely have you received. Lest Judas, who had the purse, should wish to gather money from the aforesaid power, the Lord suppresses his wickedness, saying: Freely have you received, etc. Here he also condemns the perfidy of the Simoniac heresy. Spiritual gifts become cheap by a price.
10.9: 10.9 Gold nor silver. Those who had these would seem to preach not for the sake of salvation but of gain. Nor money in your girdles. There are two kinds of necessaries: one by which necessaries are bought, another the necessaries themselves. By money in the girdles, that by which they are bought; by the scrip, what is bought, what is stored there. Of this in the passion: When I sent you without purse and scrip, did you lack anything? And they said: Nothing.
10.10: 10.10 Nor sandals. Plato also says that the two extremities of the body are not to be covered, and that softness of head and feet must not become habitual: when these have firmness, the rest are stronger. Nor a staff. Matthew and Luke say nor a staff; Mark says only a staff: by which name, etc., up to: he who ought to go the journey of preaching may be shown. He is worthy. Whence then the necessaries? Take only as much as suffices for necessity, that thereby, secure, you may be free better for eternal things.
10.11: 10.11 Inquire who. A host is to be chosen by the testimony of neighbors, lest preaching be harmed by his ill repute. Is worthy. That he may know he receives grace more than gives. There abide. AMBROSE. He gives a general command of constancy, that they keep the rights of hospitable relationship: therefore a house is to be chosen, so that there be no cause for changing lodging and breaking the bond.
10.14: 10.14 Shake off the dust from your feet. By the shaking off of dust is understood the loss of the journey. Shake off the dust, as a testimony of the earthly labor which they had undertaken for them in vain, etc., up to: they are told to have been washed through the Savior himself.
10.16: 10.16 Behold I send you. Their punishment will be kept for them in the future, etc., up to: he ought not to inflict evils, but to bear them. As serpents. The cunning of the serpent is, etc., up to: he puts off the old man.
10.18: 10.18 For a testimony. That the perverse may perish by it, etc., up to: the testimony of their own innocence.
10.19: 10.19 For it shall be given you in that hour what to speak. Offer your will for Christ; Christ will speak for himself.
10.21: 10.21 And the brother shall deliver up, etc. Evils that come from strangers cause less grief; greater those we suffer from those of whose minds we had presumed: because, together with bodily harm, the evils torture us with the loss of charity.
10.22: 10.22 But he that, etc. He teaches the virtue of longanimity and patience, etc., up to: we begin to possess this very thing which we are.
10.23: 10.23 And when. This pertains to that time in which it was said: Go not into the way of the Gentiles, that they should not fear persecutions but avoid them: so that the occasion of tribulation may be a seedbed of the Gospel.
10.24: 10.24 The disciple is not above, etc. Do not be indignant to bear what I bear, who am Lord, doing what I will, and master, teaching what I know to be useful.
10.25: 10.25 If they have called the master of the house. He shows his calumnies, that by his example they may bear injuries. Hence he said: Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof. Beelzebub. Beel is Bel himself, Zebub, fly, etc., up to: man of flies, or one having flies.
10.26: 10.26 Fear them not therefore. Their cruelty or blasphemies, because the day will come when God will judge the secrets of men, where wickedness will be uncovered, and your intention, now known to God alone, will be known to all.
10.27: 10.27 That which I tell you. That is, in which I wish you to be steadfast, etc., up to: the dwelling of the flesh being trampled, preach.
10.29: 10.29 Upon. He speaks according to the custom of Palestine, etc., up to: say in the whole world. Are not two sparrows? Luke: Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings (Luke 12)? Nor does it differ much, as two for an as and five for a dipondius. For a dipondius is of two asses. What is one in the numbers, this in weight is the as; and what is two, this is the dipondius. And one of them. How then the Apostle: Does God take care for oxen (Luke 9)? But care is one thing, knowledge another.
10.30: 10.30 Numbered. That is, the knowledge of God, etc., up to: small and idle words are hidden from him.
10.32: 10.32 Whosoever shall confess. Or one confesses Jesus with that faith which works by love; he denies who does not obey the precepts of God.
10.33: 10.33 But he that. He is denied by the Son before the Father to whom the Son and the Father is not manifested in the power of divinity. He is confessed by the Son before the Father who through the Son has access to the Father.
10.34: 10.34 Peace. A good war was sent, that an evil peace might be broken.
10.35: 10.35 For I am come. Here Luke says: There shall be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three. How then, etc., up to: circumcision and the other carnal observances. To set at variance. That is, to extinguish private carnal affections, by which they love one another in such a way that they serve God less. Or that they may be turned away entirely, not that father and mother are not to be honored, but after God; this is the order of charity.
10.37: 10.37 He that loves father. They are to be loved after God, but if both cannot be kept, hatred toward one's own is piety toward God.
10.38: 10.38 And he that takes not up, etc. The cross is borne in two ways, etc., up to: the love of Christ is shown. And follows me. For someone wastes his flesh for vain glory, or sympathizes carnally with his neighbor so as to favor fault: he seems to bear the cross, but does not follow the Lord.
10.39: 10.39 He that finds, etc. By the name of soul the present life is designated.
10.40: 10.40 He that receives, etc. When he sends to preach, etc., up to: ought to receive wages.
10.42: 10.42 And whosoever. He who announced the danger of those who do not receive by the testimony of the shaken-off dust commends the merit of those who receive beyond what was hoped. Note that God looks more to pious affection than to the quantity of the thing offered. One of these little ones. The little ones are those who have nothing at all in this world, and will be judges with Christ.
11.2: 11.2 Now John. And while Christ was preaching, etc., up to: who holds the order of the event, it does not appear.
11.3: 11.3 Are you. He does not say, who have come, as if to say: Since I am about to descend to the lower world, I must announce you to those below, I who announced you to those above. Does it befit the Son of God to die, or will you send another for these mysteries?
11.6: 11.6 Whosoever shall not be. He who has not doubted about the power of the divinity is not to be thought to have said this against John, whom he commends so highly directly afterwards.
11.7: 11.7 Concerning John. The forerunner of Christ wished to assure his disciples about Christ, because he sensed that they doubted. About the forerunner, Christ taught the doubting crowds not to doubt, who thought him soft and light.
11.8: 11.8 Behold, they that are clothed in soft garments, etc. Those who place cushions under the elbow, who stroke the life of sinners and do not sting. A rigid life and preaching ought to avoid the palaces of the soft, which flatterers frequent, dressed in soft clothes. CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA. Blessed John, despising also the fleece of sheep, which smell of delicacies, camels' hair, etc., up to: he removed himself from all vain zeal, and the empty show of goodness, and sordid and illiberal adornment.
11.9: 11.9 More than a prophet. BEDE. Because an angel not by nature but by office.
11.11: 11.11 Greater than John. In this he is not preferred to the patriarchs and all men, but is shown equal to the other saints. But he that. That is, every saint who is already with God is greater than he who is still in the world. Or, I whom the opinion of many makes lesser, am preferred to him in the Church of the saints. Or the last angel of heaven is better than any man. In the kingdom. The kingdom of heaven is understood in two ways: either the supernal, in which we are not yet; or the present Church, in which we still live, and already in a certain way reign.
11.12: 11.12 From the days of John. The Lord had ordered the apostles to go to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel, that they might be led back to the kingdom. But this preaching turned to the advancement of the publicans and sinners who believed. Moreover, John is not believed by the people, Christ's works are not authorized, because the cross is a scandal. Now prophecy ceases, now the law is fulfilled; Christ is preached to some and received by others: his own reject, enemies accept. Therefore the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, because the glory of Israel, owed to the fathers, announced by the prophets, offered by Christ, is occupied and seized by the faith of the Gentiles. Or from the days of John, who preached the presence by which the sinner revives; and not before, because the law inflicted punishment and did not give life through repentance. The heavenly homeland suffers violence when the sinner enters it by repentance as into a foreign place. It is a great violence to be born on earth and to take heaven, and to have by virtue what we cannot by nature.
11.13: 11.13 For all the prophets. Not that after John there were none, such as Agabus, but because whatever they prophesied, they foretold of the Lord. For all. Because whatever they said, they spoke of the one to come; but this one shows him coming.
11.14: 11.14 And if you will receive it. That you may be the less excusable, because you did not receive him. He himself is Elijah in virtue, not in person, equal in severity of life, preceding with rigor of mind Christ's first coming, as that one the second.
11.16: 11.16 But whereunto, etc. John being praised, he passes to rebuke those who were not moved even by John's preaching, or who despise the preaching of Christ himself. John was such and so great as I have said, and so worthy that he ought to be believed; but to whom are you to be likened, you who would not believe him? It is like to children. The children are teachers humble in spirit. Their synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, where the rights of God's commandments were stored. The fellows, the tribesmen, whom they used to reproach because they did not rise up with devout heart to the praises of God, with agility of limbs, which the leaping marks. Nor were they converted to repentance through the lamentations of the prophets for destructions already done or to be done.
11.17: 11.17 We have piped to you. As David: Rejoice to God our helper, sing aloud to the God of Jacob (Psalm 80), and the like. We have lamented. As: Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping, and in mourning (Joel 2), and the like.
11.18: 11.18 For John came. As then so now you reject both ways of salvation. We lamented to John, we piped to Christ. This is the sum. This generation neither weeps with John weeping, nor rejoices with Christ rejoicing. Nor is it wonderful if they despise the twofold way of salvation, since they spurn both fasting and fullness when sought; if fasting pleases, why does John displease? if fullness, why the Son of man?
11.19: 11.19 And wisdom is justified, etc. He shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness is neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in the equanimity of bearing want, and the temperance of not corrupting oneself through abundance. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink: of which not the use but the concupiscence is reproved; in some books it reads: Wisdom is justified by her works, because wisdom does not seek the testimony of speech but of works.
11.20: 11.20 Then. He who until now rebuked the Jews in common now expressly names the cities which, having often heard the teaching and seen so many signs, would not believe; he does not wish them evils but foretells what is to come.
11.21: 11.21 Woe to you, etc. Above, where it is read that Jesus went about all the cities and towns, healing every infirmity, it is to be understood that among others the Lord also worked miracles in Chorazin and Bethsaida. Chorazin is interpreted my mystery; Bethsaida, house of fruits or of hunters. If in Tyre, etc. We now see this fulfilled, because Chorazin and Bethsaida would not believe while the Lord was present. Tyre and Sidon afterwards believed when the apostles preached: so devoted that, when Paul was leaving Tyre, all with wives and children accompanied him to the ships. Why then did he preach to those who would not believe, and avoid those who would? He knows whose ways are mercy and truth. He had resolved, however, not to go beyond the borders of Judea, lest he give the Pharisees and priests a just occasion of persecution. And there were then some in Chorazin who were to be called; yet they were not to be punished more heavily for contempt. Tyre, distress. Sidon, hunting.
11.23: 11.23 And you, Capernaum. Woe will be not only to Chorazin and Bethsaida, but to you also, Capernaum. Shall you be exalted up to heaven? Are you not the one who became famous by the fame of my lodging and of the signs done in you, and have resisted my preaching most proudly? Capernaum is interpreted most beautiful village, in which perfidious Jerusalem is condemned, to whom it is said: Sodom your sister is justified by you, that is, by comparison of you with her, who was not corrected by the example of Lot, you have always been ungrateful for the words and miracles of the Son of God.
11.25: 11.25 Jesus answering. Answering an unspoken objection, as if it were asked: What is the reason that the Jewish people, worshipers of God, so obstinately rejected the Son of God coming in flesh, whom the Gentiles so readily received? Lord of heaven and earth. You who make the heavens, and leave in earthliness whom you will, or literally. To little ones. To the wise and prudent he does not oppose the foolish and dull, but little ones, to prove that he condemns swelling, not sharpness.
11.26: 11.26 Yea, Father. He speaks with the feeling of one caressing, so that the benefit begun in the apostles may be completed. Here we receive an example of humility, that we not rashly presume to examine the counsels from above about the calling of these and the rejection of those; for when he had brought forward both, he did not at once give a reason, but said, So it pleased God, showing that what pleases the just One cannot be unjust. In all things therefore that are arranged outwardly, the cause of reason is open, the justice of the will hidden. For so it was pleasing before you. Lest anyone again ask why he chooses the humble and rejects the wise.
11.27: 11.27 All things are delivered to me, etc. Understand mystically the Father delivering and the Son receiving. Otherwise, if you take it according to our frailty, when he who received begins to have, he who gave will begin not to have. By all things, co-omnipotent, note: by the things delivered, the Son, to whom by nature all things are proper by the right of one substance, not given by grace. But the things delivered are not heaven and earth and the rest that he made, but those who through the Son have access to the Father, and, rebels before, afterwards began to perceive the Lord. And no one knows the Son, etc. To reveal himself. And no one knows the Father but the Son, and him to whom the Son will reveal him. For that clause added refers to both. For by his Word the Father declares himself. And the Word declares himself, because he is the light of our mind. But the Son, and he to whom the Son will, etc. A mutual knowledge, which is by equality of nature. But that tiny knowledge which is in us is by the condescension of the revealer.
1.17: 1.17 So all. Having run through the order of the generation, at last, in concluding at the end, the evangelist recapitulates under a mystical number.
1.18: 1.18 Now the generation of Christ. Without addition he sets down Jesus, so that you may understand him of whom the prophet says: Your God has anointed you. Jesus, which substantially suits him, he reserves for the angel, so that he who afterwards will speak of the conception by the Holy Spirit may declare more sublimely the proper name from the office of salvation. Was thus. As was said, so that through Joseph the origin of Mary, who also shone forth from David, might be made clear; and Christ, not of his seed, is shown as God and man: man through the genealogy, God through this, that he is born of a virgin by the Holy Spirit. Thus, I say, it was as was written above and will shortly be told, as afterwards it is made manifest by signs and wonders, so that the whole book may show that God was born as man: which must be believed in order that it may be understood. For here human sense fails, where there is not nature but power: he who does not believe does not understand that a virgin gave birth, that the Word was made flesh. When she was betrothed. ORIGEN. She was betrothed in order to signify the Church, which is virgin and bride; and so that through Joseph, etc., up to: the betrothal took place some days before continual cohabitation, and meanwhile the wife was under her husband's guardianship. Before they came together. Not that afterwards they did come together, as if we said, he was overtaken by death before he repented. Not that afterwards they came together; but it shows the near time of the wedding, in which the solemnities of the nuptials are celebrated. She was found with child. Joseph found her to be with child, but did not know it was of the Holy Spirit, since afterwards, in doubt, he considered putting her away; but the apostle adds this lest suspicion should steal upon the reader in the meantime. How this came about, and in what order, or in what city the conception of Christ was celebrated, is explained by Luke, which Matthew has passed over.
1.19: 1.19 Just. Through faith, by which he believed that Christ would be born of a virgin, and wished to humble himself before so great a grace. That he was just is a testimony to Mary's chastity, since one who preserves an innocent person is called just; but he was also merciful in not wishing to expose her: just from the awareness of her chastity, merciful from fear. He knew that she was blameless, but where this came from or what it was he did not know, and so he chose a middle way of escape, that he might neither betray the innocent nor, by consenting to an unknown matter, make himself guilty before God. It is true virtue when neither mercy is without justice nor justice without mercy, which when separated from each other fall apart. And was unwilling. To take her whom he had betrothed in marriage, lest he seem to conceal what he did not know. Or to expose her to the penalty, in which he knew there was no disgrace, since he knew that he had received her a virgin and had kept her untouched.
1.20: 1.20 But while he thought on these things. Here we are taught that in uncertain matters we must deliberate for a long time, lest we sin by the rashness of levity. Behold, an angel of the Lord. Because he thinks so piously, he deserves to be consoled, and his plan is exchanged for a better plan. Son of David. Recall what was promised to the house of David, of which you and Mary are, and see it fulfilled in her. Do not fear. Although it is as great as you believe, do not fear on account of guilt, but embrace her with a look of love. Wife. She was a wife not by intercourse but by affection, not by joining of bodies but by union of souls. Note that she is called wife from the first faith of the betrothal. Therefore it is a dispensation if someone is permitted to marry another after the sacrament of the pledge, even if he could never pay the marital debt. Rightly is Joseph called husband and Mary wife, since in him the affection of love is preserved, which is true marriage, and in her, without intercourse, is the fruit of marriage. In her was born. To be born of her is to be brought forth into the light. But to be born in her is to be conceived, or according to the presence of the angel which she has from God, to whom the future is called born as though past. It is of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is called God, and the gift of God, and charity, and charity alone made him become incarnate.
1.21: 1.21 She shall bring forth. Lest Joseph seem not to be necessary to him, he adds: She shall bring forth. And so you will be necessary for the care. And you shall call his name Jesus. He says the same to him as he had foretold to Mary, so that by the voice he may show that the promised Savior has already come, to men as well as women. For he himself. The name is interpreted.
1.22: 1.22 Now this, etc. That she was betrothed to a kinsman; that she was found with child; that she gave birth as a virgin; that he was called Jesus; that he saves. The Evangelist says this when all things had already been fulfilled. That it might be fulfilled. The prophecy of Isaiah is a sign of God's foreknowledge, because what he says is certain to be foreknown by God, and therefore ought to be feared by man. But no sign effects what it designates; it only signifies what it shows; so prophecy does not impose necessity on the things it predicts, but is a sign of God's foreknowledge. JEROME. There is no necessity of things from the speech of the prophets, but only the display of the truth. Prophecy did not make necessary the things it speaks of, but is a sign of God's foreknowledge. One kind of prophecy is from God's predestination, which must come to pass in every way, so as to be fulfilled without our choice, such as this one, which is dealt with here. Another is from God's foreknowledge, with which our choice is mingled. Another is that which is called a threat, which is made as a sign of divine chastisement, so that the elect may flee from the face of the bow, and the incautious may justly perish; and it is not from foreknowledge, because what is known is far otherwise than what is threatened as future.
1.23: 1.23 Behold, a virgin. The prophet Isaiah marvels, and, as though rousing all from sleep, says: Behold, a virgin shall have in the womb (Isaiah 7). What was not yet in time was present to the Holy Spirit. Behold a virgin, etc. The Jews say that this is not the word for integrity but for age, a young girl. But how then is it a sign? He follows the sense of Isaiah, not the words. For shall conceive he puts shall have in the womb; and they shall call, for you shall call, or he shall be called. Emmanuel. This is proper to Christ, as Jesus is, since with those whom he saves he always perseveres, helping them. For three reasons he supports from the Old Testament what he sets down in the Gospel: for testification, that it may have witness from the law and the prophets; for confirmation of faith, because we believe more easily when we see fulfilled what was foretold; and for the joining of the New and Old Testaments.
1.24: 1.24 And Joseph rising, etc. BEDE. Morally: whoever is moved by God, let him cast off delays, rise from sleep, and do what is commanded. He did as he commanded. Perfect obedience. He did not only what the angel commanded, but also as he commanded. By the performance of service and the effect of love, the obedient man is rightly said to have done as he commanded him. The angel of the Lord. No room is left for lying where the office of angels is celebrated. And he took his wife, etc. To avoid the infamy of the virgin, to conceal the Savior's coming, and for the necessary service of the child to be born.
1.25: 1.25 Until she brought forth. Not that he knew her afterwards, which is the better established view, since in many ways he knew that he who was born was God. Not that afterwards he knew her; but until is used for and, or for forever, as in: Until I make your enemies your footstool (Psalm 109). It is said that Joseph could not see Mary face to face, whom the Holy Spirit had wholly filled from the conception. And so he did not know face to face her whom he had betrothed until the womb was emptied, which is not dealt with here. Firstborn, etc. Everything that opens the womb is called firstborn, whether another follows or not. Or firstborn among all the elect through grace. But properly he is called the only-begotten of God the Father or of Mary.
2.1: 2.1 Now when he was born, etc. Although Matthew passes over the nativity, yet in reporting the coming of the Magi he briefly recalls it, saying: Now when. RABANUS. Four things are set down here confirmed by the prophets: the birth, the name, the place and the time, etc., up to: Luke is silent about the coming of the Magi, and Matthew expounds it. Bethlehem of Judah. To distinguish it from the one that is in Galilee, in the tribe of Zebulun. For there are two Bethlehems: Bethlehem was first called Ephrathah; Bethlehem, house of bread, because there the Living Bread who came down from heaven was to be born, who is laid in a manger, to make the irrational beasts that are fed companions of the angels. It signifies the Church, which is the house in which the living bread is eaten. In the days. JEROME. He does not put this only for the time, but so that it may be seen as fulfilled, etc., up to: the Jews hint at the place, but do not know the time of the coming. AUGUSTINE. Jesus was manifested neither to the learned nor to the just; for it prevails, etc., up to: so that no great one might be proud, and no weak one despair. There came. The Magi, not after a year, because then he would not be found in the manger but in Egypt, but on the thirteenth day. They were from the land of the Persians, where also is the river Saba from which the region is named, near which also is Arabia, where the Magi were kings. Although they are said to have offered three gifts, it is not thereby proved that they were no more than three, but that through them the nations born of the three sons of Noah, who were to come to the faith, might be prefigured; or there were that many chiefs, who led many in their company. The Magi especially inquire at Jerusalem because they had heard through Balaam that one would be born of Israel. For a new star showed a new man. The star is Christ, whom we ought to follow, and unless he rises in our hearts, the king of the Jews is not sought in the East.
11.29: 11.29 Take up the yoke, etc. The yoke of Christ is the Gospel, which joins Jews and Gentiles in one faith. Take it upon you. That is, hold it in honor, not beneath you, that you despise it. You who labor, under the difficulty of the law, and are burdened with sins, I will refresh, namely, if you take up the yoke, that is, my precepts. And what is sweeter than his yoke? what lighter than his burden? To become approved, to abstain from evil, to will good, to love all, to follow eternal things, not to be captured by present ones, not to will to do to another what you do not wish to suffer. Learn of me. By teaching in word and example, that you may be humble in mind, meek in conduct. Humble, that they may despise no one; meek, that they may harm no one. In heart, that the same outside in work be also in the heart, lest a serpent lie hidden in the appearance of a dove.
11.30: 11.30 For my yoke. How is the Gospel lighter than the law, since there works are condemned, here concupiscence also? But in the law many things are commanded which the Apostle says cannot be fulfilled; here the will is sought, which is in our power and which alone can suffice and have reward. Likewise, how is the yoke of Christ sweet, when it is said above: Narrow is the way that leads to life? But it is narrow because it is begun only with a narrow beginning, but with the passage of time is widened by the ineffable sweetness of love. My burden. Because that which is momentary and light of our tribulation works an eternal weight of glory in heaven (2 Corinthians 4).
12.1: 12.1 At that time. Having narrated the preaching and miracles of one year done before the question of John, he passes to those which were done in another year, namely after the death of John, when Christ is now contradicted in everything. Hungry, etc. Because, as another evangelist says, they had no place to eat on account of the crowds, because of their excessive importunity. The other Evangelists add: rubbing them in their hands (Luke 6). Hence also it is said to Peter: Kill and eat (Acts 10).
12.2: 12.2 It is not lawful. According to the precept of the law. But because another Scripture says: I desire mercy and not sacrifice (Hosea 6), it was better to free a man from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God, because the pleasing victim is the salvation of men. They do not accuse them of laying waste the crops, because it is lawful by the law to eat from them.
12.3: 12.3 But he said to them, etc. In this deed we are taught nothing else than that we should understand the Sabbath not to the letter but spiritually. Have you not read. If David and Abimelech are not blamed, each of whom transgressed the commandment of the law by a probable necessity, and here there is a similar cause, hunger, why do you not approve the same in the apostles?
12.4: 12.4 The loaves of proposition. Which signified that the priestly food would pass into the use of the peoples. Or because we all ought to imitate the priests. Or because we are all priests.
12.5: 12.5 That on the Sabbath days the priests. Here he shows that the Sabbath is violated without necessity by those very ones who bring accusations. One example was given of royal power, from David; another of the priestly, from those who violate the Sabbath through the ministry of the temple, so that much less does the crime of ears of grain plucked on the Sabbath pertain to him who is the true king and priest and lord of the Sabbath.
12.6: 12.6 But I say to you. As if he said: If the figurative temple could defend the priests serving it, why can the spiritual not defend the disciples believing in it?
12.7: 12.7 And if. And to show you that all things contain the image of the future time, he added: But if you knew, that is, that God by grace has arranged to free the people, and not by exterior observances, you would not condemn my disciples if they omit the old things.
12.8: 12.8 For the Lord. If David when fed, and the priests violating the Sabbath by the ministry of the temple, are without crime, how much more the Son of man, who is the true king and priest and lord of the Sabbath?
12.10: 12.10 And behold, a man. This man is said to have been a mason, because the hand to which the care of the spiritual building was entrusted was withered until the time of Christ. Behold a man, his hand, etc. It signifies the human race withered in the fruitfulness of good work, in place of the hand stretched out to the fruit, which the innocent hand stretched out on the cross healed. Well was the hand in the Synagogue withered, because where the gift of knowledge is greater, there the transgressor is subject to greater guilt. They asked. Because he had excused the disciples by a probable example about the violation of the Sabbath, they wish to calumniate him, so that if he does not heal, they may accuse him of cruelty or weakness; or if he heals, of transgression. On the Sabbath, etc. Jesus especially on Sabbaths teaches and works, not only because of the special Sabbath, but also because of the more crowded assembly of the people, seeking the salvation of all.
12.11: 12.11 What man shall there be. With a fitting example he resolves the question, to show that those violate the Sabbath in a work of cupidity who accuse him of violating it in a work of charity. He reproves those who interpret the law badly, who say that on the Sabbath one should rest from good works. But one should rest only from evil ones; hence it is said: You shall do no servile work therein (Leviticus 23). That is, sin. So also in eternal rest they will rest only from evils, not from goods.
12.13: 12.13 Stretch forth. Because nothing is more effective for healing than generosity in almsgiving; hence it is said: Let not your hand be stretched out to receive, and closed to give (Ecclesiasticus 4). Because in vain does he who is to ask for sins stretch out his hands to God who does not stretch them out to the poor as far as he can. As the other. Before the coming of Christ man had a languid right hand, because he was torpid from almsgiving; a sound left, because he attended to his own profit; but when Christ came the right is healed like the left, because what he had greedily gathered he now distributes in charity.
12.15: 12.15 He withdrew from thence. Note the example: If they persecute you in one city, flee into another (Matthew 10). They followed. The learned persecute when they have seen his virtues; the unlearned, led by opinion of him, follow loving; hence they also deserve to be healed.
12.16: 12.16 And he charged. Not out of fear, lest he be betrayed and killed, but sparing the Jews, lest they be slaughtered by envy against his innocence and meekness. Here mystically he instructs us, that when we do something great we not seek praise outside.
12.18: 12.18 My soul. By the soul every affection is shown.
12.20: 12.20 A reed. The Jews, yielding to every wind, who were scattered by disagreeing with one another, he will not at once condemn, but will bear with. A bruised reed. He who does not stretch out a hand to the sinner, nor bears his brother's burden, breaks a bruised reed. And he who despises the small spark of faith in little ones puts out smoking flax; which Christ did not do, who rather came to seek what was lost; for he kept patience until the judgment that was being carried out in him should come to victory, and, the prince of the world being cast out, he should return to the kingdom, sitting at the right hand of the Father until he put his enemies under his feet. Smoking flax. The Gentiles, whom, the ardor of the natural law almost extinguished, the most bitter smoke of error and the harmful odor enveloped; these he did not extinguish, but from a small spark raised to the great ardor of the fire of God. Till. As long as his preaching, overcome by no snares, shines on the world, until he sets judgment on the earth, and it is fulfilled: Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.
12.22: 12.22 And he healed. Three signs were done at once which also daily happen in the conversion of men, that, the demon having been cast out, they may see the light of faith and praise God.
12.24: 12.24 By Beelzebub. Beel, that is, Baal: of flies, because of the filth of sacrificial blood; the god of Accaron, a name by which they call the prince of demons.
12.25: 12.25 Every kingdom. By a necessary dilemma he convicts them. For either Christ casts out demons by the power of God, or by the prince of the demons. If by the power of God, they calumniate in vain. If by the prince of demons, his kingdom is divided and will not stand; and therefore let them withdraw from his kingdom; which hints that they have chosen it for themselves, while they do not believe in themselves.
12.26: 12.26 And every city. The same reasoning applies to a city and a house as to a kingdom. The city of Jerusalem, always glorious, after it blazed out against Christ and the Apostles, fell in destruction, division having been made.
12.27: 12.27 And if I by Beelzebub. If the casting out of demons by your children is attributed to God and not to demons, why does the same work in me not have the same cause? They, etc. The contemptible things of the world, in which the holy simplicity of my power appears. Or rather thus: The children, that is, the Apostles, who were well aware that they had learned nothing of evil art from him; therefore they themselves will be witnesses of my judgment, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
12.28: 12.28 But if I. That part, If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, was led to many absurdities; now the other part of the dilemma is dealt with. But if I by the Spirit of God. Here Luke says: by the finger (Luke 11). The Holy Spirit is called the finger on account of the distribution of gifts. The kingdom of God: he means either himself. Hence elsewhere: In the midst of you there has stood one whom you know not (Luke 11, John 1). Or the kingdom which John and Jesus himself preached: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (Matthew 21). There is also a third kingdom of Holy Scripture, which is taken from the Jews and given to a nation yielding its fruit. Or the kingdom, that is, all parts of the world, he distributes to the Apostles and their successors for conversion.
12.29: 12.29 Or how can. The Lord therefore shows by a manifest parable that he does not agree with demons in deceptive working, as they were slandering, but by the power of divinity frees men from the demon; and therefore they commit a great crime who cried out that what they had known to be of God was of the devil. For they cannot be in agreement whose works are different. Hence he adds: He that is not with me, etc. His house. Or the house, that is, all parts of the world, he distributes to the Apostles and their successors for conversion.
12.30: 12.30 He that is not with me, etc. That is, he who does works unlike mine is against me: he draws to vices, I to virtues.
12.31: 12.31 Every sin and blasphemy. What is contracted by human frailty is remissible, if the congregation is not deserted. But if through diabolical obstinacy one never returns from dispersion to the congregation, the sin is judged unpardonable. JEROME. Every sin. Not all sins are forgiven to all, but to those, etc., up to: asserting that all will obtain pardon after the universal judgment, though many ages have passed. But the Spirit. He who manifestly understands the works of God, since he cannot deny their power, if goaded by envy he slanders and says it is Beelzebub, will not be forgiven. Not that remission is denied him if he repented, but because this blasphemer, his evil deserts demanding it, will arrive neither at remission nor at repentance. As John the evangelist says of certain men blinded by the merit of their blasphemy: Therefore they could not believe (John 10). Which Isaiah again said: He has blinded their eyes (Isaiah 6). Those who believe the Holy Spirit is not God, or is less than the Father, and say so, because they do this not from diabolical envy but from human ignorance, are not held by the unpardonable crime. But those who in the likeness of the devil, against their own conscience, assail the majesty of God, have no remission forever, as Mark plainly declares: who, having set down this testimony of the Lord, added: Because they said, He has an unclean spirit (Matthew 3).
12.32: 12.32 And whosoever. AMBROSE. Even he who, scandalized by the infirmity of my flesh, suspects me to be a mere man or a glutton, will be forgiven. But he who, not knowing the grace of the Holy Spirit by which repentance is inspired and one returns to the congregation, remains in an impenitent heart, since this is no longer human but diabolical, will not be forgiven. Neither in this world. For some faults are loosed in this world; others (the small ones, namely) even in the future. These indeed weigh upon one after death, but are also forgiven if a man by good acts in life has merited that they be forgiven there. Nor in the world to come. Because there are some light ones which, if not yet remitted in this life, weigh upon one after death, but are also remitted, if they are worthy.
12.33: 12.33 Either make. For there is no middle: the works of a good author are only good, and those of an evil author evil. He presses them from this side and that by a dilemma, and presses with both horns. If the devil is evil, he does not do good things; if they are good, they are not the devil's. Either make, etc. Mystically, the good tree is Christ; the fruit, the preaching of the Gospel; the healings, redemption. The evil tree is the devil and his own, that is, the Scribes and Pharisees; and the rest of the evil fruits: envy, detraction, blasphemy, heresy and the like.
12.34: 12.34 Brood of vipers, etc. He shows that they are an evil tree and bring forth fruits of blasphemy. Out of the abundance. Man is often deceived, who weighs the heart from the mouth and from work. But God judges the work and words from the heart, which he knows. The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart for him who knows from what intention it goes out.
12.35: 12.35 A good man. The treasure of the heart is the intention, from which God judges works, so that sometimes lesser works have greater and greater works lesser reward. In this place he either shows the Jews from what treasure they bring forth blasphemy; or it coheres with the above, that as a good man cannot bring forth evil things, or an evil man good, so neither can Christ do evil works nor the devil good.
12.36: 12.36 Every idle word. If a man will render an account for an idle word on the day of judgment, how much more you who say that the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub. GREGORY. An idle word is one that lacks either the usefulness of rectitude or the reason of a just necessity, namely, etc., up to: here he will be held guilty not of an idle but of a criminal word.
12.37: 12.37 By your words. Death and life are in the hands of the tongue.
12.38: 12.38 Then answered. When the Scribes and Pharisees could by no means disprove his words, they seek to tempt him in his works, seeking to see signs, as though what they had seen were not signs.
12.39: 12.39 But the sign of Jonas. He shows the Jews, like the Ninevites, to be guilty, and, unless they repent, near to overthrow. But as to those both punishment is announced and a remedy shown, so the Jews ought not to despair of pardon if, at least after Christ has risen from the dead, being admonished, they do penance; because the death of Christ is the reconciliation of the world.
12.40: 12.40 For as Jonas was. Jonas, that is, sorrowing, signifies him who bore our sorrows. Or dove. The fish that swallowed him in the sea is the death he suffered in the world. As he was cast out on dry land, so Christ rose into glory. Three days. In the manner of the ancients, who reckoned the day with the preceding night. Take the part of the day in which he was buried, with the past night, for the night and day, that is, for the whole day by synecdoche. The night and day of the Sabbath whole. The Lord's night with the same day dawning, part for the whole, and so you have three days and three nights. The first days are reckoned on account of the future fall of man from light into night; these, on account of man's restoration from darkness to light. Mystically: three days, three times: before the law, under the law, under grace. Three nights, three dead whom the Lord raised.
12.41: 12.41 The men of Nineveh. And the sense is: Jonas preached in a few days and without signs to an unbelieving nation, and succeeded; I preach for a long time, and to the people of God, and with very many signs, in vain. The more unworthy of pardon are those who are unbelievers from the law, as there is more faith in those who did not know the law. Nineveh, beautiful: it signifies the Gentiles, whom Christ loved foul, to make them beautiful. In the Ninevites and the queen of the South the faith of the Church is signified, which is reconciled to God no less through repentance for past folly than through the diligence of learning wisdom. For there are two parts of the Church: that which does not know how to sin, and that which has ceased to sin; for repentance abolishes sin, wisdom guards against it.
12.43: 12.43 And when, etc. As if he said: You are not like the Ninevites or the queen of the South, because when I preached repentance you did not repent, and when I taught wisdom you did not learn. But you are like the man from whom the devil, having been shut out, enters again. There is a distance between my works, which cleanse what is polluted by the world, and Satan's, who more gravely contaminates what has been cleansed. He walks through places. He explores the hearts of the faithful, purged from the softness of flowing thought, to see whether he can set foot anywhere there; because he cannot, he returns to the damp places.
12.44: 12.44 I will return into my house. He sleeps in the shade, in the covert of the reed, and in moist places. The shady shade is the conscience; the reed, fair outside, empty within, is the pretender; the moist place, the wanton and soft mind.
12.45: 12.45 Seven other spirits. Seven vices, contrary to the seven spiritual virtues. More wicked. Because he not only has vices, but also feigns good things. The more wicked, the more cunning. Seven, because so many were the graces destined with Christ. Seven vices, seven demons, contrary to the seven spirits: to the spirit of wisdom and understanding, etc. So shall it be, etc. What he said of one thing is done in this whole nation. The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the law. He went to the Gentiles, who, when afterwards they believed in the Lord, not finding a place in them, he said: I will return to the Jews, empty of the protection of God and the angels, cleansed by rebukes and corrections, adorned with superfluous observances. Seven are added, because those who blaspheme Jesus are possessed by a far greater number of demons than were those possessed in Egypt. Against the seven spirits of virtues is the number of vices.
12.46: 12.46 Behold his mother. RABANUS. Mystically: the mother and brethren are the people of the Jews, who cannot enter while Jesus is teaching inside, because spiritually his words, etc., up to: The brethren of the Lord are his cousins, sons of Mary his mother's sister, who is called the mother of James the less and of Joseph and of Jude and of Simon.
12.47: 12.47 And one said to him. Insidiously, whether he prefers the flesh to the spiritual work; and therefore he pretends not to know his mother and relatives by kinship, but says that they are near to him by union of spirit.
12.48: 12.48 Who is my mother? He does not refuse the duties owed to a mother, but prefers the services of the Father; he does not despise his brethren, but prefers spiritual work to kinship, that we also may prefer the spirit to the flesh. Hence: He that loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10). Behold my mother, etc. These are my mother, who beget me in the hearts of believers. These are my brethren, who do the works of my Father. Brother and sister by believing, mother by preaching.
13.1: 13.1 The same day. By this he indicates that this was done in sequence, unless perhaps day is put for time, in the manner of Scripture. Mark keeps the same order. Luke passes to another, but does not contradict this. RABANUS. Not only the deeds and words of the Lord, but also his journeys, etc., up to: into which the Jews did not enter, fixed outside in the letter.
13.2: 13.2 The multitude stood. These are those who lately came to hear, who also are separated from the waves of the sea, and not yet imbued with the heavenly mysteries which they desire, go up with Christ.
13.3: 13.3 He spoke many things. Because the crowd is not of one mind but of different wills, he speaks to them in many parables, that according to their various inclinations they may receive different teachings. The sower. Christ himself, who sowed among men, by himself or through his own, the word of truth which he saw with the Father. He who spoke the mysteries to the disciples went out to sow the word of God among the crowds.
13.4: 13.4 By the way side. The way is the mind trodden down and dried up by the constant passing of evil thoughts. Where the seed perishes in two ways, because it is trampled by the passing of thoughts, as Luke says, and is snatched by birds. The demons are called birds, either because of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they fly through the air. And came. According to Luke it was trodden underfoot by men, because it was taken away by the wicked persuasion of the impious. And ate. Because they stole it from the minds of men.
13.5: 13.5 Upon stony ground. Stony places quickly seek to sprout, but the root is not fixed, because the earth is not deep, that is, because there is little of saving desire in it. In this exposition of the Lord we learn that things are not always put in the same signification. For rock here stands for hardness, earth for gentleness of mind, sun for the heat of persecution. Whereas sun elsewhere is in a good sense: The just shall shine as the sun (Matthew 13), and rock in the foundation for the strength of faith, and earth for earthly thoughts. Depth of earth. The depth of earth is uprightness of soul, instructed in heavenly teachings and proved in temptations.
13.8: 13.8 Sixtyfold. Because in the number six the adornment of the world was completed, by this the good working is signified.
