13.9: 13.9 He that has ears to hear. As often as this admonition is interposed in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, a mystery is hinted in what is said.
13.10: 13.10 And the disciples coming, etc. How do the disciples come to him when the Lord was sitting in the boat? But perhaps it is to be understood that they had earlier boarded the boat with him, and standing there they ask.
13.11: 13.11 To you it is given. Note that not only the words of the Lord but also his deeds are parables, that is, signs of mystical things, which many who are outside did not understand.
13.12: 13.12 For he that has. That is, to the apostles who have faith, if they have somewhat less of virtues, it is granted; from the Jews, who do not believe in the Son of God, even if they have some good by nature, it is taken away. For they can understand nothing wisely who have not the head of wisdom. It shall be taken away from him. He will rejoice in no sweetness of true wisdom.
13.13: 13.13 Therefore in parables. It is said that they were blinded for this reason, and the sayings of the Lord were hidden from them by parables, so that afterwards they might be converted more wholesomely. For because they did not understand what was said obscurely, they therefore did not believe in him, and so crucified him, and so after the resurrection, terrified by miracles, they were pricked by the guilt of a greater crime. Hence, having received pardon, they burn with a greater love. But John speaks of this place thus: Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: He has blinded their eyes, that they should not see (John 11). Where he openly says that the blinding was not done so that, admonished by it and grieving that they did not understand, they might sometime be converted (for they could not do this unless they believed), but rather that they were blinded so that they might not believe, which they deserved by other sins. Seeing they see not. As the miser has many riches and none, because they are useless to him.
13.14: 13.14 By hearing you shall hear. These things were prophesied of the crowds, because they stand on the shore and do not deserve to hear the Lord's discourse.
13.15: 13.15 Their eyes. That is, they themselves were the cause that God closed their eyes. Lest at any time. That is, therefore, because they would not open eyes and ears, they did not deserve ever to be converted; which, however, was done to them mercifully.
13.16: 13.16 Blessed. Truly blessed, because they deserved to see and hear in person what none of those before, of however great merit, deserved, although he desired it much.
13.17: 13.17 And the just. Luke says just kings, because they rule their motions well.
13.18: 13.18 Hear you therefore. He explains the first parable, that they may attend to the same in the others. He explains not according to each word, but the sum of the meaning. AUGUSTINE on Genesis. Hence what the evangelist narrated (it was also done), namely that the Lord spoke such things. Of himself, however, etc., up to: that indeed the narrator of past things wrote, this the foreteller only of future things.
13.20: 13.20 Upon stony ground. They are sown upon rock and among thorns who receive well, but either by terrifying adversities or by flattering prosperities delay them so that they do not bring it to perfection. To riches is joined the care of keeping them, which afflicts, and pleasure, which makes them flow away.
13.22: 13.22 The deceitfulness of riches. CHRYSOSTOM. The things we have heard are choked by thorns, not indeed by the fault of the thorns themselves, but of him who them, etc., up to: for there are two vices opposed to each other in riches: one which kindles solicitude and clouds with cares; the other which makes men softer with delights.
13.23: 13.23 Another indeed a hundredfold. RABANUS. There are three differences in good ground, as there were in the bad. For thirty refers to marriage. Sixty to, etc., up to: the thirtieth of the married, because this is the age of fighters, and for these the conflict is greater lest they be overcome by lust.
13.24: 13.24 Another parable. As a rich father of a family refreshes those invited with various foods, so that each according to the nature of his stomach may take different nourishment. Hence he said another parable and not a different one, so that many are understood to follow. This parable is proposed when the crowds had been dismissed, and is explained at home to the disciples who ask. And it teaches here good will, and caution, and patience, and discretion, and longanimity, and justice.
13.25: 13.25 Men. Those who are appointed as prelates in the Church for the protection and care of others; or when the apostles receive the sleep of death.
13.28: 13.28 Will you that we go. When the spiritual man hears that this is from the devil, who can do nothing against the will of God, the wish may arise in him to remove such from the world if he has the means. But he consults the justice of God, whether he ought to do it, and whether God wishes this to be the office of men. But the Truth answers: man does not know in this life what he who now errs will be, and what his error may contribute to the good; and therefore they are not to be removed, lest perhaps those be killed who are perhaps to be; or lest it harm the good, whom they benefit, etc. It is done at the proper time, when there is no longer time for changing life and for profiting others; and then he says it is done not by men but by angels.
13.29: 13.29 And he said: No, etc. Behold patience. For hearing of the harm, he did not blaze up in anger nor wish to avenge at once; so let us too bear injuries patiently. Lest perhaps. Here a place is given for repentance, and we are warned not to cut off quickly: for he who errs today may perhaps defend the truth tomorrow. If, then, he were pulled up now, the wheat that was to be would be uprooted. Or it is necessary that the wicked be mixed with the good, by whom they are exercised. Or by comparison with whom they may strive for the better; and if these were removed, the height of charity would wither, which is to be uprooted. The wicked are to be patiently tolerated where some are found by whom the good are helped. AUGUSTINE. A multitude is not to be excommunicated, nor the prince of the people.
13.30: 13.30 Suffer. This seems contrary to the apostolic: Take away the evil from among you (1 Corinthians 5). But as between the cockle and the wheat, as long as it is an herb, there is little difference, so the Lord warns us not to judge about what is ambiguous, which the Lord on the day of judgment will condemn not with suspicion but manifestly. In suffering let us meditate on justice; in judging let us not neglect justice. And in the time. He who bore long through justice renders what is due; for the virtues are distinct but not contrary. And bind. In this life there is no binding; otherwise not so many would come to their senses from error.
13.31: 13.31 The kingdom is like, etc. The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel, of which elsewhere: The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation yielding the fruit thereof (Matthew 21). Or the knowledge of the Scriptures. A grain of mustard seed. It is compared to a grain of mustard seed for the fervor of faith, because it is said to expel poisons, that is, all doctrines of wickedness. In the grain of mustard seed the humility of the Lord's incarnation can be understood. Which a man took and sowed in his field, because Joseph, taking the body of the crucified Savior, buried it in a garden. He spread out branches in which the birds of the air will rest, because he scattered the preachers into the world, in whose words and consolations the faithful might breathe again from the weariness of this life.
13.32: 13.32 But when it is grown up. In the whole world or in the mind of each; because no one is suddenly perfect. It grew and became a tree, because he rose and ascended into heaven. Or grown, that is, when it becomes known to the minds of men how great is its power. The other things appear as herbs, which quickly grow and decay: not vigorous but withered; that one becomes not an herb but a tree, where leaves with fruit, and in its various sentences the spiritual rest. Among herbs and becomes a tree. That is, the doctrines of philosophers, which quickly grow and decay, promising nothing of life.
13.33: 13.33 In three measures of meal. That spirit, soul and body, brought into one, may not disagree among themselves. Or the three powers of the soul are brought into one, so that in reason we possess prudence, in the irascible hatred of vices, in the concupiscible desire of virtues. Or, the woman, the Church, mixes the faith of men with three measures of meal, belief in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. And when it is leavened into one, it leads us not to a threefold God but to the knowledge of one divinity, because there is not a different nature in each. Until it was leavened. Charity stored in the mind must grow until it changes the whole mind into its own perfection, so that it loves or remembers nothing besides God; this is begun here, in the other life is perfected.
13.34: 13.34 In parables to the multitudes. Because whatever is said there about the army of Israel, and all the signs, are hidden mysteries.
13.44: 13.44 A treasure hidden in a field. The treasure can be taken as the word of God, which is hidden in the flesh of Christ. Or Scripture, in which the knowledge of the Savior is stored up. Or the two Testaments in the Church, for the understanding of which all things are renounced that they may be learned in leisure. The kingdom of heaven is likened to earthly things, that through the known the mind may rise to the unknown and love. He hid it and for joy thereof. That it may be guarded from malign spirits and from the praises of men. Let the work be in public, in such a way that the intention remains hidden.
13.45: 13.45 To a merchant. The beatitude of which we were stripped by the fault of the first man we must all trade for, by understanding rightly and working well. Good pearls. The good pearls are the law and the prophets. One precious, the knowledge of the Savior, for which man, like Paul, renounced all the mysteries and observances of the law.
13.46: 13.46 And having found. That is, Christ, who presides over all men, or the spiritual precept of love. Or the word understood, which was with God, the shell of the flesh having been penetrated. Or the sweetness of the heavenly life, for which all things become cheap.
13.47: 13.47 A net cast. The prophecy of Jeremiah is fulfilled: Behold I will send many fishers to you (Jeremiah 16). After Peter and Andrew, James and John heard: Follow me, I will make you fishers of men, they wove for themselves a net from the Old and New Testament, and cast it into the sea of the world, which is drawn even to this day and stretched in the waves, catching whatever falls into it, good and bad, which it draws to the shore, that is, to the end of the world, so that then the division may be made. Hence follows: So shall it be at the end of the world, etc. The Church or the evangelical preaching is compared to the net, which draws from the waves of the world to heaven.
13.48: 13.48 And by the shore. The shore, the end of the age, in which the good will be sent to heaven, the wicked to darkness; for in the present they were mixed.
13.52: 13.52 Therefore every scribe instructed, etc. Because you understand the mysteries which I reveal to you, therefore I will make you preachers, and you will be like me, who bring forth from the treasure of my knowledge new things and old, that you may do likewise. The apostles are the scribes and notaries of Christ, signing his words on the tablets of the heart, and are strong with the wealth of the father of a family, bringing forth from the treasure of their teachings new things and old, because whatever is preached in the Gospel they confirm by the voices of the law and the prophets.
13.54: 13.54 So that they wondered. A great blindness: they who recognize Christ by his words and deeds despise him because of knowledge of his family.
13.55: 13.55 The carpenter's son. Not without reason did he wish to be called the carpenter's son, not of the one they think, but of the maker of all. But the Jews, ignorant of this mystery, despise the works of divine power from regard for his carnal lineage. For they do not consider his present works, but remember his frail infancy.
13.57: 13.57 A prophet. Christ is called a prophet. Hence Moses says: The Lord will raise up a prophet to you of your seed (Deuteronomy 18). In his own country. That is, among the people of the Jews; but he does greater things among the Gentiles.
13.58: 13.58 And he did not. He did some miracles, but not many, lest he condemn the unbelieving. Or, despised, he does few, lest they be altogether excusable, but he does greater among the Gentiles.
14.1: 14.1 At that time Herod heard. Luke thus: Now Herod the tetrarch heard (Luke 9), etc. So what he said: This is John (John 4). Either he said it confirmed by the opinion of some after hesitation, or still doubtful; for these words fit either.
14.2: 14.2 And he said. Note the envy of the Jews. Here a foreigner says that John, who did no sign, has risen; they contend that Jesus, approved by so many miracles, has not risen. And therefore. For they perceived that the saints rising from the dead would be of greater power than when burdened with frail flesh.
14.3: 14.3 For Herod. Because he spoke of the opinion of the resurrection when he had said nothing of the death, he returns and tells how and why he died. This Herod and Philip were brothers, sons of Herod, under whom the Lord fled into Egypt. Herodias his wife. Herodias, the daughter of King Aretas, whom her father himself took from Philip and, to his grief, gave to Herod, his enemy.
14.4: 14.4 It is not lawful. Herod perhaps held the law of the Jews, and therefore John was forbidding him from adultery.
14.5: 14.5 He feared the people. He feared the people, but love overcame, for which he even put God aside. The fear of God corrects; the fear of men delays but does not take away the will; hence it makes more eager for crime those whom it at times holds back from crime.
2.2: 2.2 Where is he who is born king, etc. It is the confusion of the Jews, that they learn from the Gentiles where Christ was born; and if they do not believe, they are without excuse. For we have seen the star. This star, the herald of the Lord's nativity, never appeared before; the child created it then and assigned it to the Magi, and once its office was done it soon ceased to be. The mute star proclaims Christ while he is not yet speaking; afterwards, when he spoke, the apostles announced him to the Jews, as to those who use reason. A rational substance, that is, an angel, announced the birth of Christ; but the Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles who did not yet use reason, an irrational one, that is, a star, led. Angels to the shepherds, a star to the Magi; yet to both the language of heaven speaks, since the language of the prophets was now ceasing. Whether the star arose in the East, or they, being stationed there, saw it born in the West, is uncertain. For it could have been born in the East and led them to Jerusalem. But while they seek human help as though by law, they are abandoned by the divine. Through the star they understood that he was born in Judea, and so they come to Jerusalem, where, learning the place, they set out on the journey and have the star going before them, which they recognize. Allegorically: the star is the illumination of faith which leads to Christ. While they turn aside to the Jews, they lose it, because while they seek counsel from the wicked, they lose true illumination. LEO. The three men follow the guidance of the heavenly light and, accompanying the sign of the preceding brightness with intent contemplation, come to the knowledge of the truth, etc., up to: so that the mystery of so great a vision might not be hidden from them, and what was shown to the eyes as unusual might not be obscure to their minds.
2.3: 2.3 And Herod hearing, etc. He is called king so that, by comparison with him who is sought, this one may be understood to be a foreigner, since their own king had already failed. And Herod hearing. That another king of the Jews than himself was being sought; for being a foreigner he wished to be seen as the lawful king, and therefore he burned the books in which the genealogy was recorded. He was troubled, etc. Either because he feared the end of his kingdom, or because of the anger of the Romans if he allowed this, who had decreed that no one should be called king or lord without their counsel. At the birth of the King of heaven, the king of earth is troubled, because earthly loftiness is thrown into confusion when heavenly highness is proclaimed. With him. Out of favor: because the people often favor unjustly those whom cruel men support. Hence Solomon: A king who listens to lies has all his ministers wicked (Proverbs 29).
2.4: 2.4 And gathering together all the chief priests. Note the diligence of the inquirer, so that if he finds him he may do what he shows he wishes afterwards; but if not, he may be excused to the Romans. He also tested whether their king would make the Jews sad or glad. Where Christ should be born. He asks the place from the Jews and the time from the Magi, that he may be certain of both.
2.5: 2.5 In Bethlehem of Judah. They state the place of the nativity, which they learned from the testimony of Scripture, so that their very knowledge would become for them a testimony of condemnation, and for us a help to faith. From this it is plain that they refused to believe not from ignorance but from hardness of heart.
2.6: 2.6 And you, Bethlehem. He sets this down as it was said by them, because even if they do not give the words, they give the truth of the sense in some way.
2.7: 2.7 Having secretly called the Magi. The priests and scribes having been removed; for he feared lest the Jews, as though from an oracle of God, should conceal the promised one if they sensed that he wished to destroy him. For this reason also he promised to adore him, so that no one should perceive his guile, but they might report to him without suspicion for the sake of his favor.
2.8: 2.8 That I also may adore him. Herod promises devotion, but sharpens the sword, painting the malice of his heart with the color of humility. He pretended with face and words to adore him whom with envious mind he planned to kill. His person is represented by hypocrites, who seek God falsely and never deserve to find him.
2.9: 2.9 And behold, the star which they had seen. Having entered Judea they are deserted by the indication of the star, so that they are compelled to inquire from the law. Or those who seek human help are abandoned by divine help. Nor was it fitting that a sign given to unbelievers should appear to those of the household of the law and the prophets; for if they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they if one rises from the dead, etc. It did not keep to the ethereal paths but came very near to the house, otherwise they would not have distinguished the house. Morally: the star is good exhortation leading to Christ. Or rather faith, which is the illumination of the mind, by which one who enters sees Christ, who is the morning star; and having seen him, he rejoices with joy and does not cease to adore.
2.10: 2.10 They rejoiced with great joy, etc. He rejoices with joy who rejoices on account of God, who is true joy. He adds also great, than which nothing is greater. And exceedingly, because of a great thing one can rejoice more, another less.
2.11: 2.11 And entering the house, etc. Three Magi come by one journey to adore God, because in one Christ, who is the way, the inseparable Trinity was to be adored by them. The child with Mary his mother, etc. He is often named child, so that they may recognize him of whom it was said: A child is born to us. Why was Joseph not also found with Mary by the Magi? Lest any occasion of evil suspicion be given from this to the Gentiles, who sent their firstfruits at once to adore the Savior when he was born. They adored him. Thus confessing as God him whom they understand to have been made man, and who would die, which they show through myrrh. And opening, etc. They declare their faith by mystical gifts: closed gifts are the faith of the heart; opened gifts, etc., up to: or through these three things are intimated in the same Christ: royal power, divine majesty, human mortality.
2.12: 2.12 And having received an answer. As Moses cried out while silent, so these with pious affection were asking what the divine will commanded. This answer is not given through an angel but through God himself, because no one else established the way of return except him who says: I am the way, the truth, and the life. The child does not speak to them, lest the divinity be revealed before its time, and that true humanity be held. Hence he is soon sent into Egypt: because faith had to be nourished for the reward, and the life of teaching had to be prepared for going forth. By another way, etc. In this a pattern is given to believers, that they come devoutly to God and attend to what he commands, namely, not to return to the devil but to come to the homeland by the paths of virtues, and that those who fell by contempt may rise by obedience. LEO. They adore in the flesh the Word, in infancy wisdom, in weakness power, and in the truth of man the Lord of majesty, etc., up to: because what was proper in the substances was not different in the person.
2.13: 2.13 Take the child, etc. HILARY. When he signified her as betrothed to the just man, he called her wife; but after the birth she is shown only as the mother of Jesus, so that just as the marriage of Mary in virginity was assigned to the just Joseph, so the virginity of the mother might be shown venerable in Jesus.
2.14: 2.14 Who rising. Joseph is a figure of the preachers, who carried Christ with his mother, that is, the faith of Christ and the Church, to the Gentiles, leaving Herod, that is, the unbelief of the Jews. By night. Because he went down secretly by flight to enlighten Egypt, leaving the night to the Jews. He took him by night into Egypt, because he left the night of ignorance to those unbelievers from whom he withdrew. When he returns, no mention is made of night, because at the end of the world the Jews, receiving the faith as Christ returning from Egypt, will be enlightened. Into Egypt, and was there, etc. It shows God venerated by every kind of people: because Christ, not received by the Jews, passes through preaching to the Gentiles. He fled into Egypt as he was born, to repair corrupted nature. He fled so as to call back the fugitives. That he fled was of mystery, not of fear, to give his own an example of fleeing. He who had come to die did not flee death, nor did he who had come to uncover the wiles of the devil fear plots. Isaiah foretold this flight: Behold the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, that is, flesh without sin, and he will enter Egypt (Isaiah 19). He lay hidden in Egypt seven years. Out of Egypt I have called. This is found in Hosea according to the Hebrew truth, or in the book of Numbers, as some assert, because the whole was done by God's arrangement.
2.16: 2.16 Then Herod seeing. It is likely that, since nothing had been reported to Herod by the Magi, he believed they had been deceived by a false star and therefore had not returned to him; hence he rested so long from searching for the child. Then, when the things that had been done and said in the temple became widely known, he perceived that he had been mocked by the Magi, and, hastening to the death of Christ, he killed the children. It is likely that Herod raged against the children a year and four days after the birth of Christ; he perhaps delayed because he had set out for Rome, either being accused there, or to consult the Romans about what was being said of Christ. Perhaps for this reason he refrained so long from searching for the child, that he might seize him more carefully and he could not slip away in any manner. He killed all the boys. As soon as Christ appeared to the world, persecution began against him, which prefigured the persecution of the saints; and while the infant is sought, infants are killed, in whom the pattern of martyrdom is born, where the infancy of the Church is dedicated. The death of the little ones prefigures the passion of all the martyrs, who, as little ones, humble and innocent, were killed; who suffered not only in Judea but everywhere at the hands of the impious, whom Herod signifies. Two years old: because perfect in doctrine and work. When they were killed Christ escaped, because bodies can be destroyed, divinity cannot be touched. And in all its borders. He was not content with the devastation of Bethlehem but laid waste the adjacent places; and he had no mercy for age, killing all from the son of one night to the son of two years. From two years old. For this reason from two years old: that, as Herod had seized beforehand the borders of the city, so he might also anticipate another year. Also from two years old because he feared that the child, whom the stars served, might make himself appear a little above or below his age.
2.17: 2.17 Then was fulfilled. It is said fulfilled because before it came to pass it was half full for readers, since what sounded in the letter secretly promised something to come. CHRYSOSTOM. He says that the star appeared for a year, as in the destruction of the Romans signs appeared in the sky, when the voice of angels was heard: Let us depart from these seats.
2.18: 2.18 A voice in Rama. That is, on the height it was spread far and wide. Allegorically: or, the voice of the Church groaning over the slaying of her members goes up to the throne of the supreme judge. A voice in Rama. Because of the Levite's wife killed through fornication and divided into twelve parts according to the number of the tribes, all Israel destroyed the tribe of Benjamin except three hundred men; the weeping and wailing of those who survived was heard as far as Rama, which is a place near Gibeah, twelve miles from Bethlehem. Heard. He exaggerates, so that by hyperbole Rachel, though already dead, is said to weep for her sons with the feeling of one grieving. Hence from this a history is woven concerning the Chaldeans: that a devastation like the earlier slaughter of the people of the Jews would be brought by them. But more truly, the Spirit revealing it through the evangelist, the prophecy is taken as concerning the slaying of the children. He says therefore that then was fulfilled what was said, because although the prophetic speech looks to the imminent captivity, yet in it, as in a shadow, the future truth of the slaughter of the infants is proclaimed. Rachel. Because she was buried near Bethlehem, and from the earthly lodging of her body she received the name of mother. Or because many of Benjamin and Joseph were killed. From Rachel was born Benjamin, to whose lot Bethlehem does not belong, but only to the tribe of Judah. But because the tribes of Judah and Benjamin are adjacent in the territory of Bethlehem, many also of the tribe of Benjamin were killed. Note that it is better (than if Bethlehem were said to weep) that a figure of the sacrament is conveyed through Rachel, because through her in all things the pattern of the Church is commended, which weeps not so much for those translated by death as for those slain by torment. Rachel, that is, the Church, weeps for her tender lambs slain, and does not wish to be consoled in the present, because they are not; but sends all hope and consolation on to eternal life. The Church weeps and does not wish to be consoled here, because her sons are not of this world. Or she weeps because, while she gives birth, she has righteousness; hence it is said: You shall weep, etc.; but consolation is added: Your sorrow shall be turned into joy (John 16).
2.19: 2.19 But Herod being dead, behold, etc. Because the perfidy of the Jews will be lulled to sleep, and with Elijah and Enoch preaching, Judea will receive the word of God. When the king is dead his accomplices straightway perish; so, persecution ceasing, the Church is invited to heavenly things.
2.20: 2.20 Into the land. He does not specify to which part, so that the angel may return while Joseph is in doubt, and Joseph be made more certain by his frequent address. Because he did not distinguish to which part, Joseph therefore understood Judea, which was the worthier part of the kingdom. Of the dead. Some relate that Herod had the nobler of the Jews killed at his funeral, so as thus to compel the Jews to weep for his death.
2.21: 2.21 Who rising. Allegorically: Joseph bears the figure of the apostles, by whose office Christ is carried about. The apostles first came into the land of Israel, because they first preached to the Jews. But on account of Herod, that is, the abiding hereditary unbelief, they fear and withdraw, admonished to preach grace to the Gentiles and to carry Christ over to them. The land of Israel having been named, it seemed to Joseph that such a child ought to dwell nowhere except in Jerusalem, where the temple was and the worship of the prophets. Yet the angel wished Galilee to be understood, which the Jews also inhabited, which shows that it was so predestined, because he shall be called a Nazarene.
2.22: 2.22 He was afraid to go there. If he feared Judea on account of Archelaus, the heir of his father's cruelty, why not also Galilee, where Herod, another brother of his, reigned? Because Archelaus after his father held the rule of the whole kingdom; but growing insolent, he was deposed by Tiberius Caesar and sent into exile at Lyons, and then the kingdom was divided into four tetrarchies, of which his brother Herod held one, namely Galilee. The question is: why did Joseph not fear to go into Galilee as into Judea, since Archelaus reigned there too? But he could better lie hidden in Nazareth, which was remote, than in Jerusalem, where was the head of the kingdom and Archelaus constantly. He withdrew into the parts. That Christ is not carried to where Archelaus reigned signifies that Christ will be hidden from those in whom Antichrist will reign.
2.23: 2.23 Nazareth. Nazareth is interpreted a young shoot or flower of the field, from the root of which shoot the Holy of Holies is read to have ascended, to signify the substance of his eternity. As he chose the time and place of his birth, so also the city in which he would grow up, whose name is a sign that holiness itself, nurtured in holiness, is rightly called the Holy of Holies; hence his disciples were first called Nazarenes, but afterwards were called Christians from Christ. Nazareth of Galilee, to which he is transferred, signifies the part of that nation which was going to receive the faith; hence it is interpreted flower, because the more ardently the Church migrates from earthly to heavenly things, the more she abounds in the flower and shoot of virtues. By the prophets. He says prophets in the plural because we do not have a fixed example from Scripture; it shows that he took the sense, not the words. Or in the same words in Isaiah according to the Hebrew truth: A Nazarene shall rise from his root (Isaiah 11).
3.1: 3.1 Now in those days. He passes over much and moves to the preaching of John. In the days. He includes not only the years of boyhood but all up to John's preaching, that is, when Jesus was almost thirty years old. Luke expresses the times more significantly: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Preaching. He who had been silent before made himself manifest by baptizing, preparing the way for the Lord. In the desert of Judea. Because the Jews were forsaken by God, for whom penance is necessary, that they may return.
3.2: 3.2 Repentance. The herald announces this, which afterwards Truth itself announces in person; repentance goes first, the promise of the kingdom follows: he who truly repents, first condemns in himself past errors, then lifts his mind to the heavenly kingdom. If remission is given freely in baptism, why is repentance preached? But there is a threefold mode of repentance. The first is to renounce and condemn errors and all evils before baptism, which is necessary for those about to come to Christ. The second is that those who have fallen after baptism be called back by repentance. The third is that by which the saints are daily cleansed from those sins without which life is not lived. To repent is to weep over past deeds and not to commit what is to be wept over. To the penitent the kingdom of heaven is said to be at hand; not earthly things, as in the old law, and this through the obedience of Christ. And this kingdom of heaven John first preached: Do penance. The first virtue is to destroy the old man by repentance and to hate vices; whoever does not do this not only fails to grasp virtues but does not even escape punishments. The virtue of repentance is conceived by fear, which is the beginning of wisdom. Repentance (paenitentia) is from punishing (puniendo), by which each punishes what he has unlawfully committed. To do penance is to bring forth worthy fruits of repentance. The kingdom of heaven. That is, Christ, through whom the saints reign in heavenly places. Or the Gospel, by which he invites to the kingdom. For it is at hand, etc. Unless it drew near, no one could return, because the weak and blind lacked the way, which is Christ; John, preparing it, puts it before the penitent.
3.3: 3.3 The voice of one crying. John is the voice, Christ the Word, who cries in John. No word is heard without a voice, nor does a voice avail without the understanding of the word. The voice prepares the way for the word, that it may be received. Hence: I have prepared a lamp for my Christ (Psalm 131). In the desert. A pattern for penitents: the place of life is not the crowds of men but the desert. His clothing not soft for display but rough; his food slight and unusual. Typically, the desert signifies the life of the saints set apart from the allurements of the world. The way of the Lord. The way of the Lord is directed to the heart when his speech is diligently heard.
3.4: 3.4 And John himself. He who preaches repentance displays the garb of repentance. In him the plainness of clothing and food is praised, the use of which is blamed in the rich. John himself in his own person instructs penitents and presents a pattern of life, dwelling in the desert, living on locusts, wearing camel's hair. The servant of God ought to have clothing not for beauty or delight but only to cover nakedness. Hence John was clothed in hair.
3.5: 3.5 Then went out to him, etc. Because unless one goes out from evils he is not washed. Hence it fittingly follows: They were baptized by him in the Jordan, which is interpreted descent, because they descended from the pride of the old man to the humility of confession and amendment. For already then an example was being given to those to be baptized of confessing sins and promising better things.
3.6: 3.6 In the Jordan. Because in it the figure of baptism went before, and by its name it demands descent from pride, which suits the baptized. Confessing. The confession of sins is the testimony of a conscience fearing God. For he who fears the judgment of God is not ashamed to confess his sins. More perfectly, fear removes all shame. Confession of sin has shame, and the blushing itself is a heavy penalty. Therefore we are commanded to confess sins, that we may suffer the blushing as a penalty. For this itself is part of the divine judgment.
3.7: 3.7 Many of the Pharisees, etc. These are among the sects of the Jews, and the Pharisees put forward the righteousness of observances and traditions. Hence the Pharisees are so called, that is, separated from the people by a private righteousness. The Sadducees, that is, the just: for they claim for themselves what they are not; they deny the resurrection, saying that the soul dies with the body; they receive the five books of Moses and reject the prophets. John rebukes these as they come to baptism, because they most needed correction and repentance. Brood of vipers, etc., that is, poisonous sons of poisoners, because they envy the good and persecute them, and harm their neighbors like their fathers. The viper kills its father; so the Jews killed the prophets, who were their fathers.
3.8: 3.8 Bring forth therefore fruits worthy. BEDE. As though he said: Why do you not first put away your poisons, that so to baptism, etc., up to: it is grace that perceives, and perceiving seeks holiness.
3.9: 3.9 For I say. He draws them back from the flesh, that they may think of the works of God's predestination. The first rudiments of faith are to believe that God can do whatever he wills, that he who created all things from nothing can form sons of Abraham from stones or from dust. Of these stones. Pointing to those stones which Joshua had carried over from the Jordan, toward which, as though stretching out a finger, he speaks. Joshua had twelve stones carried from the midst of the Jordan to the land, and others from the land set in the same bed; by these the blinding of the Jews and the transformation of the Gentiles to the light is foreshadowed. Or he calls the Gentiles stones; and the sense is: Do not boast of the seed of the flesh, for only these are the sons of God who are enlightened by grace and raised up inwardly. He says raise up pointedly, because Christ took Sarah, that is, the Church, and by grace raises up sons to Abraham, who had died without children, so that so great a patriarch might not be deprived of the promises. In foreshadowing of this matter, God long ago begot a son from Sarah.
3.10: 3.10 For now the axe. Lest they should seem immune if they separated themselves from such sacraments, he threatens. The axe is Christ, who consists of handle and iron, that is, of humanity, by which he is held, and divinity, because it cuts. It is laid: because although he waits through patience, he sees what he is going to do. At the root. That is, at the end of the Jewish people, that he may remove from the land of the living those who do not believe in Christ. Or the axe is the sentence of judgment, or the preaching of the Gospel. At the root. Note: not at the branches but at the root. For when the sons of the wicked are taken away, what else than the branches of a fruitless tree are cut off? When the whole offspring is taken away together with the parent, the tree is cut off at the root, lest anything remain from which a shoot might spring up again. The roots are thoughts, by which those planted are either raised up to heaven or sent down to the depths of hell. The tree is the human race: of its branches, some are dry, that is, pagans, fit for burning; others green but without fruit, like hypocrites, who put on the appearance of holiness but are empty within; others fruitful but poisonous, that is, heretics, who by preaching bring forth fruit, but deadly; others, that is, Catholics, who bear good fruit. Every tree, therefore: like the Gentiles and hypocrites, who bear none, and heretics, who bear bad.
3.11: 3.11 I indeed. Lest he seem to threaten on his own authority, he begins to disclose how great is his dignity whose presence he threatens with, or whose benefit he persuades of: I indeed baptize you in water. I wash only bodies, for I cannot loose sins; that as I run before in being born and in preaching, so also in baptizing, so that I may direct the penitent, whom I distinguish by this sign from the impenitent, to the baptism of Christ. He that shall come after me. Although I admonish you to bring forth worthy fruits of repentance and to cast away pride, I cannot however release from sins. He is mightier than I. Because I baptize unto repentance, he unto remission. I have the spirit, he gives it. I preach the kingdom of heaven, he gives it. Whose, etc. Others write: The strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to loose. John could have said both, either in sequence or at different times, so that one evangelist took up this, another that. Yet all told the truth. He intends in this to show the excellence of Christ and his own humility. Or according to allegory: the sandal is the mystery of the incarnation; the strap, the binding of the mystery. John therefore cannot loose the strap, because he is not able to search out the mystery of the incarnation. Or, I am not worthy to loose the strap of his sandal, that is, I do not usurp for myself the name of bridegroom, nor wish to be believed or called the bridegroom, but the friend of the bridegroom. For it was the custom that if anyone refused to take as wife the woman who was due to him, the one who would come to her as bridegroom by right of kinship loosed his sandal. John therefore, who is not the bridegroom, says: I am not worthy, etc. As though he were to say: I am not able to uncover the footsteps of the Redeemer, because I do not usurp the name of bridegroom. Or he simply humbles himself, or he is not worthy to bear about by preaching the sacraments of the Gospel, which was not assigned to him but committed to the apostles. I am not worthy to unfold the nature of the Divinity in relation to the humanity. Or, I am not worthy to carry the preaching of the Gospel, or to usurp the name of bridegroom. John, as a mere man, could not give the Spirit, by which guilt is remitted. But Christ gives it, because he is God; and he baptizes in the word, of which it is said: And you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you (John 15); and elsewhere: Cleansing it by the washing of water in the word of life, sanctified (Ephesians 5). In the Holy Spirit. Or the spirit of sanctification, and fire, that is, the testing of tribulation. Or in the present he washes by the Spirit; afterwards, if any stain has crept in, he burns it to purity by purgatorial fire, which is to be believed of lighter sins. Hence in Leviticus a fire sent from heaven always burned upon the altar, that is, the fire of divine love, which as it were rebaptizes and burns away the vices of the flesh of all who are in Christ, that is, who are offered upon the altar.
3.12: 3.12 Whose fan. The fan in the hand is the examination of judgment by which the light and those empty of the fruit of good work are discerned. In his hand, because the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son. He will thoroughly cleanse, that is, he cleanses daily from various temptations. Or, He will thoroughly cleanse, when the perverse are cast out of the Church for manifest sins, or condemned after death. The chaff. Chaff arises from the same origin as wheat, that is, from seed, but tares from a different one. The chaff therefore are those who are imbued with the sacraments of faith but are not solid; the tares are those who are separated from the elect both by work and by profession. Of these it is said: He who does not believe is already judged, and so no mention is made of them here. Unquenchable. Because it will not be extinguished, nor will it extinguish those tormented, but will punish eternally. It is said to distinguish it from that of which it is said: You have tried us with fire (Psalm 65), etc.
3.13: 3.13 Then Jesus comes. When John was preaching and baptizing, namely when Jesus was thirty years old, showing that no one should become a priest or preacher unless of a useful age. As Joseph at thirty took the rule of Egypt; David began his reign at that age; Ezekiel merited prophecy. Jesus came for these reasons: to approve the baptism of John, and (because he was man) to fulfill all righteousness and the humility of the law; and, sanctifying the waters, to show by the dove at the washing the coming of the Holy Spirit. For he came not out of need of washing, but so that no one, however holy, might judge the grace of baptism superfluous. From Galilee to the Jordan. Galilee, transmigration; Jordan, descent. Whoever therefore wishes to be baptized, let him migrate from vices, and descending be humbled.
3.15: 3.15 Suffer it now. Suffer me now to be baptized by you, that afterwards you may be baptized in the Spirit for what you ask of me. For it is fitting to give an example of fulfilling all righteousness, that all may learn that no one is perfect without the water of baptism. Then he suffered him. When he had learned that righteousness was to be fulfilled in such an order. He suffered him, because it is true humility which obedience, its companion, does not forsake. The Spirit taught him in a moment what he did not know before, and so what he first feared humbly he fulfilled devoutly.
3.16: 3.16 And Jesus being baptized. Christ sanctified the waters of baptism, because it belongs to the same one to create and to sanctify. As man consists of two, that is, body and soul, so he is reborn by two: water, which purges filth and buries together with Christ, and the fire of the Spirit, by which, set ablaze, we are caught up to heaven. So the Church after baptism seeks the summit of virtues by certain increases, as Christ, baptized, came up out of the water. So those who advance in virtues come up after baptism, and those who were first carnal and sons of Adam become spiritual and sons of God. The heavens were opened, etc. And this for the fulfilling of righteousness. For it was not then for the first time that the heavens were opened to him or the Holy Spirit given, but he showed that through baptism received the entrance of heaven is opened to us and the Holy Spirit given. For that the heavens were opened, that the Holy Spirit came, that the voice of the Father sounded, etc., these mystical things are in us. The entrance into heaven, which was closed through Adam, lies open to the reborn through Christ. Like a dove. He had a true body formed for the hour in the species of a dove, because otherwise the Spirit could not be seen by men as a dove; not that it was a true dove, but that the Spirit was in bodily form, though not itself a body. So we understand of this figure as of others in which God appeared, which were dissolved when their office was fulfilled. Rightly the Spirit descended in a dove, simple and gentle, to indicate both the simplicity of his own nature, and him upon whom he descended as a mild herald and giver of mercy. Likewise all reborn by baptism ought to be filled with the seven virtues signified in the dove. The dove is free of the malice of gall, in which we are forbidden anger. It harms none with beak or claws, in which innocence is noted. It does not attack even the smallest little birds, on which other birds nourish themselves and their young: in which we are forbidden rapine. It feeds on pure grain, in which abstinence is noted; it cherishes the young of others as its own: behold charity. It gives groaning for song: behold compunction. It sits by the waters so that, seeing the hawk's shadow in the waters, it may turn aside: behold watchfulness. In the dove the Spirit appeared over the Lord, because he came to gather us by gentleness; over the disciples in fire, whom he came to set ablaze against themselves to consume the rust of sin. Adam by sinning lost heaven; Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit and appeared through the dove; the water of baptism extinguished the flashing flame that barred the way, because water is contrary to fire. I am well pleased. That is, I have established my good pleasure, that you, in whom nothing but good pleases, and through you others, not in themselves but in you, that is, united to you by faith and glory, may please.
4.1: 4.1 Then Jesus. After baptism, because there is no delay from temptation, so that he may soon teach the baptized to go out from the world and be free for God in quiet; so the children of Israel after the crossing of the sea go up through the desert and eat manna until they come to the promised land. Then Jesus was led, etc. RABANUS. This is the order of right conduct, that after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit we gird ourselves more closely against the devil; by that way the Samaritan descended, because clothed in flesh he endured the same temptations. By the Holy Spirit, who sends strong to the battle those whom he fills. Without this spirit, whoever goes to the battle soon falls. To be tempted by the devil. He is not tempted by the devil unless because he has gone out to the desert, that is, has begun to pursue what is good.
4.2: 4.2 And when he had fasted. BEDE. He fasts that he may be tempted; he is tempted because he fasts; and he gives us the example of fasting, etc., up to: and so as long as we are here, let us always weep for sins, because by this number the present life is shown. LEO. While the care of this life is stretched out through various activities, it is necessary that from worldly dust, etc., up to: that in whose resurrection we are raised together, in his passion we may be found dead together. Afterwards he was hungry. This belongs to true humanity, and through this there is occasion for temptation. His power lies hidden, his weakness is plain.
4.3: 4.3 And the tempter coming. Because hunger is a sign of weakness. And so in abstinence temptation is not lacking to us. Through exterior weakness he tempts Christ, in whom he found no law of sin. If you are the Son of God. One of these belongs to one probing, the other to one tempting, when he seems to confess God and tries to mock him in this fashion. For he tempts so as to probe what he fears. He probes so as to deceive by tempting. If you are the Son of God. He knew that the Son of God had come into the world, whether through the prophets or through angels announcing, or through John pointing him out; but because he saw lowly things in him, what he suspected about the Deity came into doubt for him through pride. Hence he also inquires craftily. Nor was it unworthy that Christ be tempted, who had come to be slain, that by overcoming temptations he might give us power to overcome temptations, as by his death he took away our mortality. RABANUS. Christ allowed himself to be tempted only after baptism, hinting that those who go to him will suffer graver things, etc., up to: but Christ was tempted by suggestion alone, because the delight of sin did not bite his mind.
4.4: 4.4 It is written. He does not use power but the authority of the Scriptures, teaching us to fight rather by doctrine than by miracles. Not in bread alone does man live. As if: Your persuasion is a temptation, because you speak of the food of the body and not of the food of the mind. The lower part of man is sustained by bread; the other is refreshed by the word of God; because you speak of the lower, it is plain that you are a tempter. But in every word, etc. Every word is charity, in which are fulfilled all things that proceed from the mouth of God, because by whoever's ministry they are spoken, they are not his but God's; but if anything contrary is inserted, this is not of God. Whatever the saints who are his mouth speak proceeds from the one Word, that is, the Wisdom of God.
4.5: 4.5 Then took him. The first and last temptation were in the desert, the middle one also historically; the last was after he returned to Jerusalem. Because Matthew follows not the order of the history but the temptation of Adam; Luke follows as the event happened. Because he was defeated and left uncertain by Christ's reply, after the first he came to the second temptation. That he allowed himself to be taken was not weakness but patience; in the devil, not power but pride. Note that all these things were accomplished with bodily senses. Nor is it wonderful if he allowed himself to be carried about, if the taking is so understood, he who allowed himself to be crucified. Upon the pinnacle. RABANUS. In Palestine the roofs were flat on top, and there was the seat of the teachers, whence, etc., up to: he shows that we should obey whoever commands us good and lofty things, but oppose anyone who wishes to cast us down. If you are the Son. BEDE. In all the temptations he acts so as to understand, etc., up to: it is likely that the devil appeared in the form of a man. Cast yourself down. This word suits him who is eager to cast all down; in this he is shown weak, that he can harm no one unless that one first throws himself down. For he suggested that he should probe by some sign how much he could do with God. But no one ought to tempt God when he has from human reason what he can do. Hence, though he could do all things, he says to his own: If they persecute you in this city, flee into another. And he himself fled and went away and hid. Now he could have come down from the temple otherwise than by throwing himself down in boasting. After human reason fails, let man commend himself to God, not by tempting but by devout confession. For he has given his angels charge of you. BEDE. What is rightly said of the body, the devil wrongly interprets of the head, etc., up to: but he speaks of the help of angels as to a weak man, and is silent about his own trampling.
4.8: 4.8 Again he took him. This temptation came earlier in order but is told out of order, according to what was done to Adam. He showed, etc. Not that he enlarged the sight of him who sees all things, but he showed the vanity of worldly pomp which he loved, as being beautiful, etc., up to: Not that he looked upon it with an eye of concupiscence as we do, but this showing was in the mind, as physicians see diseases without being harmed.
4.9: 4.9 All these will I give you. He says this out of arrogance, not because the whole world is his. From the beginning the devil labored to usurp for himself what was God's; hence, to be worshiped in them, he invented idols. In these three are marked gluttony, avarice, pride. RABANUS. Luke puts avarice in the middle and pride last, etc., up to: in these three all kinds of temptations are comprehended.
4.10: 4.10 It is written. David struck down Goliath with three stones from the brook, and Christ the devil with three testimonies from the law. The Lord your God. This is either said to the devil, not because he would fulfill it out of devotion, but so that, on the contrary, what he himself was contriving might be shown to be written, that not he but God is to be adored; or he hints that this precept is not for the devil but for himself according to his humanity, and for any man. Likewise also that: You shall not tempt the Lord your God, namely the Son and the Father and the Holy Spirit, who is one God. God is adored, and is served specially for his own sake. Here it is shown that Christ as man, as God and Lord, is to be adored as a debt. You shall serve. In Greek, douleia is the word for servitude. Servitude common to God and man and anyone is called douleia in Greek. But that which is owed to God alone is called latria; hence idolatry, which gives to idols what is owed to God alone. Note that the devil is conquered in these things in which Adam was conquered. Whom he tempted with gluttony when he asked him to taste of the forbidden tree; with vainglory, when he said (Genesis 3): You shall be as gods; with avarice, when he said: Knowing good and evil.
4.11: 4.11 Came. Not as though then approaching for the first time, but watching the Lord's contest from afar, lest he seem to have needed their protection or to have won by it. But when the other had departed conquered, they came ready to serve. As in this contest our warfare is prepared beforehand, so in the service of the angels a glorious reward is taught.
4.12: 4.12 Now when he had heard. RABANUS. Here Matthew, like Mark and Luke, passes over the Lord's first coming into Galilee, after, etc., up to: This beginning of signs Jesus made. And again: John was not yet cast into prison. John, etc. Which was for the Gospel. Jesus, preaching the same thing more perfectly, yields for a time and flees, that he may be an example to his own. Into Galilee. There are two Galilees: one is called of the Jews, the other of the Gentiles because of the dwelling of Gentiles, which part Solomon gave to the king of Tyre, who settled Gentiles there.
4.13: 4.13 Nazareth. RABANUS. From which Christ is called a Nazarene; it is a village in Galilee near Mount Tabor, etc., up to: because in the midst of the Gentiles he stands firm to spread the word of God, to show those in danger who believe the harbor of faith as a refuge.
4.15: 4.15 The land of Zabulon. The same. The evangelist passes over what was put first, namely: At the first time the land of Zabulon and the land of Nephthali was lightened (Isaiah 9); as also what is in the middle, etc., up to: but for a figure of those who are to be called from the Gentiles, that which is of the Gentiles is mentioned here.
4.16: 4.16 The people. AUGUSTINE. This people, who were first led into captivity and were in the darkness of vices, first saw the light of Christ's preaching. Then the Gospel was spread to all. Hence follows: To those sitting in the region. Of the shadow of death. Death is in hell. The shadow of this death is sins, which are never without death. Whoever therefore wishes to flee death, let him avoid the shadow.
4.17: 4.17 From that time. After he was baptized. Baptism makes fit for preaching. From that time, that is, John having been delivered up: because when the law ceases the Gospel follows, as the sun follows the dawn. A humble master, who does not hinder the teaching of the disciple but waits until he finishes his course. In which he teaches that no one should despise a discourse from an inferior person. Hence the Apostle: If anything be revealed to another sitting, let the first hold his peace. Do penance. The same things the herald preaches, to show that he is no other than he who had cried out in the voice. For Christ is the word that cries in the Jordan through that instrument and in all who from the beginning have said anything by divine inspiration; and yet this one alone is the voice, because through him the present word is shown which others announced from afar. For between voice and word there is nothing in between, but as soon as the voice has sounded, the word is perceived; as John, shut up, ceased, Christ shone forth in miracles. Hence John is a figure of the prophets and the law, who are truly the voice of Wisdom of God crying out, whose end John is, and when they cease the Word alone, who had sounded in them, is shown by himself. RABANUS. This preaching of Christ, begun in Capharnaum with flashing miracles, is said, etc., up to: he began to preach when the Baptist was imprisoned.
4.18: 4.18 Who is called Peter. Or when Andrew first brought him, this name was given him, when it is said: You shall be called Cephas (John 1), which is interpreted Peter; though here he seems to promise it as future. Or when he confessed: You are Christ the Son of the living God, it was said to him: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church (Matthew 16). BEDE. Peter, obeying; Andrew, manly: which suits teachers, because these alone, etc., up to: because the first man went out disobedient, the second entered obedient. RABANUS. Matthew says he called the disciples after dwelling at Capharnaum. John says, etc., up to: but before Jesus came to Cana of Galilee, Andrew brought Peter, but they were not yet disciples. Casting a net. Because those whom he sees often gaping after earthly gains he calls to heavenly desires, and through them with the nets of the Gospel he rescues others from the depth of iniquity; hence he adds: Come after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men (John 1).
4.19: 4.19 Fishers. He who is about to fish goes through fishing places. Mystically: when, made incarnate, he took flesh, he saw by divine sight in the sea of the world spiritual fishers, and showed to others what they were, whom he foresaw from eternity.
4.20: 4.20 Immediately. It is perfect obedience to leave one's imperfect things. Leaving the nets: because even if they afterwards take them up again, it is not out of cupidity and love of ownership. In these a pattern is given to those who wish to follow. The intention is changed, not the fishing; the nets are changed into doctrine, cupidity into love of souls; the world becomes the sea, the Church the ship, the fish good and bad men.
4.21: 4.21 He saw two other brothers. Behold, in these four the number of the evangelists is prefigured, who draw souls out of the world from the four parts of the world. They are called two and two, because charity exists only between two. It is called a calling: either according to the election of grace; hence it is said: Whom he called (Romans 8), etc.; or according to that: Many are called (Matthew 10). AUGUSTINE. The question is how Matthew and Mark say that Jesus called them in pairs: first Peter and Andrew, etc., up to: and he sent unlettered fishermen to preach so that faith might be thought to be in the power of God, not the eloquence of men. Zebedee and John. Zebedee is a fugitive, that is, the devil. James, the supplanter, who is helped by John, that is, by the grace of God. And he called them. But they, etc. He called others too, but it suffices to name these.
4.23: 4.23 And Jesus went about all Galilee. Having called his helpers, he gives himself to preaching, teaching that a teacher ought to be unwearied. Teaching in their synagogues. Teaching morals to those subject to the active life; preaching about future things to the perfect of the contemplative life. Teaching natural justices, namely chastity and humility and the like, which man has naturally. Preaching the Gospel of the kingdom. To the Gospel belong the mystery of righteousness, a good beginning, the promise of beatitude, the remission of sins, adoption, resurrection, the heavenly inheritance, the company of the angels. In the synagogues. A teacher should not run about idly in vain but preach where there are more people. The Gospel. Because righteousness is a burden to one living in the flesh, the labor of righteousness is not undertaken unless the reward of the work is expected. Therefore Christ proclaims beatitude, to rouse to patience in good work. And healing. To cure languor and infirmity was no great thing, since they would die later. But it was done so that they might thus be lifted up to the kingdom. Morally, instructing preachers to minister even earthly help to those under them, and so to draw them to the kingdom.
4.24: 4.24 And his fame went abroad. BEDE. Works of salvation without the report of a good odor do not shine sufficiently for the hearers, nor does report profit without the work: without which, etc., up to: he heals bodies, that they may more readily hear invisible things. Otherwise it was of little worth to bestow care on those soon to die.
4.25: 4.25 There followed. AUGUSTINE. The crowds were of four kinds, namely: some, etc., up to: others, out of envy, wishing to accuse him and to catch him in something.
5.1: 5.1 And seeing the multitudes Jesus. AUGUSTINE. Luke agrees with this, saying: And it came to pass in those days that he went out into the mountain to pray (Luke 6), etc. But Luke says, etc., up to: for not all can do all things; which is held to be truer, although the same thing can seem to have been done by both at once. He went up. Teaching his own to go up and not remain in the crowd, about to teach a higher righteousness than that of the Scribes and Pharisees. The mountain itself goes up into a mountain, to teach the higher summits of virtues, and to show that the Church, above which he sits preaching the Lord's precept, must be raised higher, which the same doctrine would instruct more fully until the end of the age. He leads the apostles up more eminently, that first from the mountain the mountains may receive peace for the people. He sat down. The sitting of the humanity, through which he is known. Hence: And the world knew him not, before the incarnation. His disciples came. That they might hear more closely, who hasten in mind to fulfill.
5.2: 5.2 And opening. The opening of the mouth signifies the depth of the mystery. As if he opened an abyss, as if a treasure, as if the river of paradise. On this mountain he writes the New Testament in the hearts of the sons, beginning from beatitude, he who on Mount Sinai gave the Old Testament on stones to servants, beginning from terror. AUGUSTINE. The sermon which our Lord spoke on the mount, as in the Gospel, etc., up to: Everyone who hears these my words and does them, I will liken him to a wise man (Matthew 7).
5.3: 5.3 Blessed. GREGORY OF NYSSA. Beatitude, in my opinion, is the comprehension of all those things which, etc., up to: for misery is hardship in bitter and sad events and calamities which do not befall by our will. Blessed are the poor. The number of the sayings is to be carefully attended to. For beatitude begins from humility. JEROME. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Because not necessity but faith and devotion to poverty make blessed, etc., up to: as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so poverty is the beginning of beatitude. CHRYSOSTOM. The poor in spirit are the humble and contrite in heart. By spirit he here meant the soul and the will. But since many are humble not willingly but constrained by necessity, he calls the first blessed.
5.4: 5.4 Blessed are the meek. The meek are those who rule over evil habits; the possession of morals is perfect virtue. THEOPHYLACT. The meek are not those who do not become angry at all, etc., up to: so the teaching of a man is discerned through patience. They shall possess the land. AUGUSTINE. I believe that land to be the one of which it is said in the Psalm: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living (Psalm 161).
5.5: 5.5 Blessed are they that mourn. For their own sins or those of others, which comes from the lower watering; but that which comes from the upper watering is from desire for the heavenly homeland. The former washes away present stains, the latter kindles more keenly the lovers of eternal things. But he who has laid aside sins, corrected his morals by meekness, and also wept, can now hunger and thirst after righteousness, which he could not before. This virtue is not fulfilled without the spirit of fortitude, because through it, by hungering, we shall come at some time to fullness. Blessed are they that mourn. It remains, after the aforesaid, to purge the filth of ruins by mourning. Mourning for sins or for heavenly desire merits consolation, and no other. These are enlightened by the spirit of knowledge, that they may know in what evils they are entangled. HILARY. For those who mourn, not bereavements, or insults, or losses, but who weep for old sins and are burdened by the conscience of the crimes with which we have grown foul, this diligent consolation is prepared in heaven.
5.6: 5.6 Blessed are they that hunger. Lovers of the good word, for whom it is not enough that they are just, but who always thirst for the work of righteousness. Righteousness is to render to each his own: to oneself, to neighbors, and to God. This righteousness will not be fully satisfied until God is all in all; therefore here we can hunger, not be filled. The light of righteousness is mercy, the virtue of mercy is righteousness; this mercy needs the spirit of counsel, without which no one has mercy circumspectly. The beginning is to have mercy on oneself, the end is to die for another. For the order of mercy is that each begin from himself. Christ hints at the end, dead for sinners out of mercy.
5.7: 5.7 Blessed are the merciful. Mercy is born of the preceding things: for if true humility has gone before and the mind grows gentle, and weeps over its own and others' falls and hungers for righteousness, afterwards true mercy is born. Then it will make others' miseries its own and help according to strength; and if the ability to help is lacking, compassion will not be lacking: Be merciful as your Father also is merciful (Luke 6), that is, be merciful for the same purpose for which God is, that goodness may overflow upon all. Mercy without righteousness is called laxity and lukewarmness; righteousness without mercy, severity and harshness.
5.9: 5.9 Blessed are the peacemakers. RABANUS. The peacemakers are those who compose all movements of the mind and subject them to reason, because nothing resists these who are like the Father, etc., up to: but when God will be all in all, then the beatitude of adoption will be given.
5.10: 5.10 Blessed are they that suffer persecution. In the seven aforesaid is the showing and proof of perfection. Those who have the aforesaid things can suffer persecution; and he rightly holds what he has received who is ready to die for them.
5.11: 5.11 Blessed are you when they shall revile you. Up to this point he set down the sayings generally, as if to those absent, though they also pertained to those present; now he turns his words to them (although this too applies to others), foretelling how much they would suffer for his name, because he wished to make known to them the dignity of their rank, saying: You are the salt of the earth, you are the light of the world; so that from sad things they might receive humility, from glad things consolation. Shall revile. The old translation has: When men shall hate you, and shall say all evil, and shall cast you out. The sense is the same in ours, since curses come from hatred of the heart. He who desires the glory of heaven does not fear reproach on earth; as much as anyone rejoices in the praise of men, so much he is saddened by reproach. Whom praise lifts up, blame casts down; where one seeks to be praised only before God, he does not fear to be confounded in the sight of men. Lying. He adds this lest one glory in that of which evil is truly spoken. He also adds: For my sake, because sometimes false things are said, which happens by the rashness of men, yet they do not suffer this for Christ, whom they do not follow.
5.12: 5.12 For your reward is very great in heaven. Not in changeable things, since the eternal reward ought not to be in changeable things, but in spiritual firmaments, where eternal righteousness dwells. Already therefore those feel this reward who rejoice in spiritual goods. But it will be perfected when this mortal shall put on immortality. For so they persecuted, etc. He tempers by example the rigor of the passion. Persecution is done in three ways: by hatred of heart, by words, by deeds.
5.13: 5.13 You are the salt of the earth. Here now the office of the apostles is shown, namely that they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. This is said specially to the apostles, who ought to be adorned with the aforesaid virtues, poverty and the others, that they may be the best salt, seasoning others by doctrine and the example of their life. Salt, salvation from corruption. Hence the prophet: I have set you for a light of the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation to the ends of the earth. But if the salt, etc. That is, if you, by whom others are to be seasoned, fail in adversities or prosperities, by whom will error be taken away from you, when God has chosen to take you from others? It is good for nothing, because (as another evangelist says) it is neither useful for the land, which it forbids to germinate by its being thrown on it, nor for the dunghill, which it does not allow to be fertile. So he who goes backward neither bears fruit himself nor is able to cultivate others, but is cast out of the Church, and is laughed at with these words: This man began to build, and was not able to finish. If the salt shall lose its savor (Luke 4). That is, if the teacher through fear or desire loses the savor of wisdom, by whom will his foolishness be amended? This suits the apostles alone; what follows, all masters: It is good for nothing any more, etc. At the end he concludes about all thus: Unless your righteousness abound, etc. And to be trodden under foot by men. The holy and true minister of Christ, even if he is laughed at by the wicked, cannot be trodden down, because, fixed in mind, he remains in heaven.
5.14: 5.14 You are the light of the world. Salt before light, because life comes before doctrine; life leads to the knowledge of truth. He who fears God does not lack knowledge. Light of the world. There is another reason why they should not fail: because, enlightened by Christ in word and example, wherever they are brought they must minister the light of faith and knowledge to worldly people. And as (because they are salt) they must drive away corruption, so also (because they are light) they must put darkness to flight. A city cannot, etc. Because the apostles are foundations, they are fittingly called a city. Upon a mountain. The place hints at the mountain of righteousness, which is lofty, where you are made known that you may not hide yourselves. For there is no ability to evade or to do anything secretly; therefore govern your subjects mercifully within by counsel, and defend them outside against adversaries by fighting for righteousness; which belongs to the spirit of counsel and fortitude.
5.15: 5.15 Neither do men light a lamp. He teaches by domestic examples not to hide the light of the word entrusted to them. They do not light, that is, the teaching of preaching was not given in order that they hide it and subject it to the servitude of the body while they fear something. But let them subject their body to the ministry of God, that through the voice and the other offices of the body the light may appear more excellent than the rest. Hence it is said in 1 Corinthians 9: I chastise my body, etc. Or, Christ lit a lamp when he filled the earthen vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity; this he did not hide from believers, nor enclose under a bushel, that is, the measure of the law, or within the bounds of one nation. But upon a lampstand, that is, the Church, he fixed the faith of his incarnation, where all can see who are in the house, that is, the Church, or in the world. Hence he adds: So let your light shine, etc. Lampstand. As Christ is the lamp, the lampstand is the cross, upon which he was to be lifted up. The lampstand is the Church, which bears the word of the present life.
5.16: 5.16 So let your light shine, etc. And do all these things in such a way that you do not set the end of the good work in the praises of men. That they may see, etc. I require works that they may be seen, and so the teaching confirmed; and this not for your glory.
5.17: 5.17 Do not think. After he has exhorted them to suffer all things for the truth, and not to hide, and to make the glory of God, he begins to teach what they are to teach. As if he said: What is it that you forbid to be hidden, for which you order all things to be suffered? Is it something against the law? I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill it, either by doing what it says, or by supplying what was lacking and imperfect.
5.18: 5.18 One jot. BEDE. Here it is shown that what are thought the least things in the law are full of spiritual sacraments, and all, etc., up to: because iota signifies ten, that is, the Decalogue, whose summit is the perfection of the Gospel. Till all be fulfilled. Let them be fulfilled spiritually, or let imperfect things be perfected, and let signifying things be consummated, that is, by fulfillment.
5.19: 5.19 He therefore that shall break, etc. The least things are the cross of Christ and his passion; whoever is ashamed of it is least; whoever confesses it is great. Or he marks the Pharisees, who set aside the commandments of God for their traditions, which are worth nothing, while they pass over even the least thing that is in the law. Morally, he breaks who does not fulfill but holds them as given to the weak. Or who does not understand spiritually. To break is not to do what one rightly understands, or not to understand what one does not distort, or to diminish the integrity of what Christ has added. He shall be called least, etc. In the kingdom of heaven he will be called least who will be unworthy in it, in which none is least but all are great. But he that shall do. He who does not break and so teaches is not least, yet not great, but does what he teaches. For only the doers of the law are just before God (Romans 2).
5.20: 5.20 For I say to you. When he says, I say, he has struck a great force and a deep understanding of thinking; he shows how he adds. And he does not abolish what he had commanded before. It is even more to love enemies than not to hate; not to desire than not to commit adultery; not to be angry than not to kill. Unless, etc. That is, unless you fulfill not only the least precepts of the law, but also those which I add; because while the additions are made for perfection, these also, which were put first for the beginning, are more fully done; because he who does not look at a woman to lust after her does not commit fornication, nor does he kill who is not angry. Your justice. He calls the justice of the Pharisees all those things commanded for the worship of God in act, or the mystical things of figures instituted only to the letter.
5.21: 5.21 You have heard, etc. He explains what the justice of the Pharisees is, which he who fulfills is not at once great, but climbs some step.
5.22: 5.22 But I say, etc. He begins to explain the perfection which he came to fulfill, and how their justice ought to be exceeded. Whoever is angry. Because they did not know that homicide was anything but killing, he discloses that every movement of the mind toward harming is reckoned as homicide. The commandment of Christ is not contrary to the law, but contains the law more broadly in itself. He who is not angry does not kill. But not conversely, a license to be angry as a cause of homicide. Take away anger, and homicide is not done.
5.23: 5.23 If therefore you offer your gift. He explains the fuller justice by showing that if it is not lawful to be angry with a brother, much less to retain in the mind what seeks to be turned into hatred. If we have anything evil in mind against our neighbor, we cannot offer pleasingly to God. If therefore you offer. According to the letter this is absurd. There is therefore in the inner temple an altar, that is, faith, upon which any gift, that is, psalm, hymn, prayer, and the like, unless it rests on it, will not be pleasing to God. And there, etc., that is, when in the heart (which is the inner temple) you are about to offer such a gift, if it comes to mind that your brother has something against you, whom you have injured. For if he himself injured you, he does not have something against you, but you against him; and then you need not ask pardon but give it, as you wish to be forgiven.
5.24: 5.24 Leave there, etc. He does not say take it back, because what is rightly offered may not be changed. But leave it, until you may offer more acceptably; for he does not reject the gift but seeks the neighbor's charity, without which no one comes to the charity of God. Hence: Let him who desires his gift to please God first render charity to his neighbor. Go. Not with the feet, but let him humbly prostrate himself in mind before him in the sight of him to whom you are about to offer. Or by asking pardon if he is present. You shall offer. This is from the spirit of piety by which one becomes meek, and devoutly understands the divine word, obeys by understanding, and lifts the heart to fulfilling.
5.25: 5.25 Be at agreement. As he has already commanded to be reconciled to a brother, and afterwards orders enemies to be loved, so here, while we run in the way of this age, he exhorts to peace and concord, as it is said: If it be possible, as much as is in you, having peace with all men (Romans 12). And in place of at agreement, from the Greek one has kindly or well-disposed. Quickly: do not put it off until tomorrow. While you are in the way, while it is still possible to work. If you have injured a brother, be reconciled to him. If an adversary has arisen, be well-disposed, that he may become a friend. In the way with him. The divine word is with us in the way of Christ. The adversary is with us in the way of the age. The divine word is for us the way in which we run. Hence: I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart (Psalm 118). Lest perhaps he deliver. He so moderated it as not to leave out a place for repentance: for it might be thought that if the adversary died and one could not be well-disposed to him in the way, he would necessarily be handed over to the judge. But he left a place for repentance, and handed the impenitent over to the judge, saying: The judge deliver you to the officer. Deliver, that is, be the cause why you are delivered into the hands of Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment. Christ to the officer, that is, the angel, who will gather the tares.
5.26: 5.26 The last farthing. That is, the small sins, because nothing will be unpunished. Or by the last farthing earthly sins are signified, because the first part of the world is heaven; the second, air; the third, water; the fourth, last, earth. Therefore until you pay the last farthing, that is, until you atone for the sins you contracted from the earth.
